findings.headline: Worthing's treasury budget significantly underspent partly because project interest was capitalized to avoid revenue overspend on Integrated Care Centre
findings.detail: Worthing's treasury management budgets were 'significantly underspent' in 2025-26, largely due to capitalization of interest on the Worthing Integrated Care Centre Project. Paper notes 'had this interest not been charged there would have been an estimated £300k overspend in treasury management.' This accounting choice avoids revenue impact on a major capital project but masks underlying financing pressure.
findings.matters: Interest capitalization deferred revenue pressure; without it, the council would have faced a £300k overspend on treasury costs, indicating tight affordability margins on this major project
findings.figures: £300k potential revenue overspend if interest not capitalized; actual treasury underspend due to capitalization
findings.quote: Overall the treasury management budgets for Worthing were significantly underspent for the financial year 2025/26. This was largely as a result of the capitalisation of interest chargeable on the Worthing Integrated Care Centre Project. Had this interest not been charged there would have been an estimated £300k overspend in treasury management.

findings.headline: Energy price shock threatens further inflation spike and rate increases: treasury advisors flag risk of CPI breaching 4.5% later in 2026
findings.detail: Economic summary notes 'recent upward pressure on energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later this year' and warns 'the Middle East conflict is likely to see inflation spike higher from late spring 2026 through to early 2027.' This directly counters the previous expectation of rate cuts. Higher inflation would force Bank of England to hold or raise rates, increasing borrowing costs. Public finances are already under pressure with government debt interest at highest levels since June 2025.
findings.matters: If energy-driven inflation spike materializes, refinancing costs will be significantly higher than currently budgeted; lenders assess councils' resilience to sustained high rate environment
findings.figures: CPI February 3.0% (peaked July-Sept at 3.8%), forecast potential breach of 4.5%, government debt interest payment highest since June 2025 at £13.0bn
findings.quote: inflation concerns remained elevated in March 2026...the recent upward pressure on energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later this year...the Middle East conflict is likely to see inflation spike higher from late spring 2026 through to early 2027

findings.headline: Interest rate environment sharply reversed from expectation: Bank Rate held at 3.75% and treasury advisors now expect rises to 4-4.25%, not cuts
findings.detail: Initial interest rate forecasts in early 2025 expected 'gradual reductions in short, medium and longer-term fixed borrowing rates.' Actual outturn: Bank Rate reduced only to 3.75% and inflation concerns prevented further cuts. By 31 March 2026, 'the market expected Bank Rate to increase over the coming months to 4% or 4.25%' with 'all parts of the curve risen substantially through March.' PWLB rates: 1-year 5.04%, 5-year 5.28%, 10-year 5.72%.
findings.matters: Refinancing of maturing debt (23-25% of portfolio under 12 months) will occur at materially higher rates than forecast; both councils face higher financing costs and must refinance debt when rates are elevated
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75%; 1-year PWLB 5.04%; 5-year PWLB 5.28%; 10-year PWLB 5.72%; 23-25% debt matures under 12 months
findings.quote: Interest rate forecasts initially suggested gradual reductions in short, medium and longer-term fixed borrowing rates during 2025/26. Bank Rate did reduce to 3.75% as anticipated, but the initial expectation of significant rate reductions did not transpire, primarily because inflation concerns remained elevated in March 2026. At the start of April 2026, the market expected Bank Rate to increase over the coming months to 4% or 4.25%

findings.headline: Worthing's two £5m housing loans to Worthing Homes mature in 2027 and 2028, ending £70k annual net revenue contribution
findings.detail: Worthing made two loans of £5m each for 10 years to Worthing Homes to support housing delivery. The council receives £70k per annum net (above the cost of PWLB borrowing). These loans mature in 2027 and 2028. This income stream is temporary and will end within 12-24 months, potentially impacting treasury returns and requiring replacement investment strategy.
findings.matters: Loss of £70k annual net revenue income from maturing loans reduces recurring income available for council services; lenders may scrutinize replacement capital spending plans if housing programme cannot absorb the loss
findings.figures: Two £5m loans, total £10m, £70k annual net return, maturity 2027 and 2028
findings.quote: Worthing Borough Council has made two loans of £5m each for 10 years to Worthing Homes to support   the building of homes.   The Council receives £70k per annum net in interest over and above the cost to the Council of borrowing the £10m from the Public Works Loan Board...The loans are fully secured on property and mature in 2027 and 2028.

findings.headline: Chichester College restructured debt during 2025-26, requiring Worthing to obtain independent legal advice on its £5m loan security
findings.detail: Worthing made a £5m loan to GB Met College (now Chichester College Group) in January 2020 for 20 years to support local education. During 2025-26 the college restructured its wider debt, triggering Worthing to seek external legal advice (costs borne by the college). Advice concluded 'no material changes' but the college's new financing is 'in part secured on the same site' as Worthing's loan, with Worthing's security ranking 'ahead of other creditors'. The fact that restructuring occurred and legal review was necessary signals counterparty financial stress.
findings.matters: Counterparty financial weakness (requiring debt restructuring) on a £5m 20-year loan creates repayment risk even with first security ranking; lenders may be concerned about covenant compliance and the college's operational sustainability
findings.figures: £5m loan advanced January 2020, 20-year term, security ranking: first creditor position
findings.quote: During the 2025/26 year Chichester College Group restructured other elements of its debt, impacting on some elements of the original agreement. Officers sought advice...which concluded that there were no material changes to the terms of our loan agreement. The new loan financing agreed by the college, is in part secured on the same site as the loan made by this council, however WBC's security continues to rank ahead of other creditors

findings.headline: Major capital schemes reprofiled out of 2025-26: Southwich FC (£3.6m), Shoreham Harbour Walls (£2.8m), Daniel Close/Gravelly Crescent (£1.7m) and others
findings.detail: Both councils experienced significant capital underspends due to extended lead times and staff resource constraints. Adur budgeted £19.043m but spent only £14.551m (24% underspend). Worthing budgeted £21.566m but spent £21.111m. The paper attributes delays to 'extended lead times and staff resources on the ability to deliver some projects.'
findings.matters: Persistent capital delivery delays raise questions about execution capability and could affect forward borrowing plans and capital strategy credibility with lenders
findings.figures: Adur capital underspend £4.492m; Worthing capital underspend £0.455m; reprofiled schemes total at least £8.8m
findings.quote: the difference between the current budget and the actual spend is attributed to: re-profiling of budgets including large schemes where works will complete in a future year such as: £1.7m Small Sites schemes at Daniel Close and Gravelly Crescent £3.6m Southwich FC Football Ground Redevelopment...£2.8m Shoreham Harbour Walls

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: 35% of audit recommendations remain in progress after due date; 2 not yet started
findings.detail: Of 122 audit recommendations that have reached their due dates, only 66% are reported by management as complete or superseded. 41 recommendations (35%) remain in progress and 2 have not started. This indicates slow implementation of audit findings across both councils.
findings.matters: Delayed implementation of audit recommendations suggests weak governance prioritization - when remediation of known control weaknesses is pushed beyond due dates, it indicates management focus is elsewhere rather than on financial control improvement.
findings.figures: 122 due recommendations: 81 complete (66%), 41 in progress (35%), 2 not started; plus 83 previously reported complete recommendations verified and closed during follow-up
findings.quote: Of 122 actions that have reached their due dates, 81 (66%) have been reported as closed by management (Complete or Superseded) with a further 41 (35%) partially actioned (In Progress) and two not yet started.

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: General ledger reconciliations lack formal secondary review process and audit trail requirements
findings.detail: Academy feeder system reconciliations do not include audit trails showing who performed and approved each reconciliation; GL reconciliations do not formally specify or document where secondary review is required. Implementation is being coordinated by the Senior Systems Accountant across multiple departments.
findings.matters: GL reconciliation is a critical compensating control for financial reporting accuracy - without formal secondary review capture and audit trails, errors or inappropriate entries have increased risk of going undetected.
findings.figures: Not specified; due 31/07/2026
findings.quote: General ledger reconciliations should be reviewed to specify, and formally capture, where secondary review is required to reduce the risk of errors/inappropriate action going unnoticed.

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: Council tax reductions lack documented approval audit trails and quality checks
findings.detail: Case note audit history is not maintained for council tax reduction decisions, and no spot checks are conducted. The councils are implementing percentage-based checks of revenues work as remediation, but this indicates a control gap in a key revenue stream.
findings.matters: Undocumented approvals of tax relief without quality assurance increase fraud and error risk in a material revenue source - poor controls here directly affect cash flow and financial position accuracy.
findings.figures: No volume specified; percentage-based checks to be implemented; due 30/11/2026
findings.quote: The Councils should ensure that case note audit history is maintained regarding the checking and approving council tax reductions, including details of officers involved. Spot checks should be undertaken at regular intervals to act as quality assurance on case history.

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: IT vendor risk management left incomplete; full policy implementation deferred due to LGR time pressure
findings.detail: Internal audit found significant gaps in IT third-party risk management: missing vendor risk guidance, no centralized due diligence documentation store, and no periodic risk reviews of critical suppliers. Management agreed to create guidance documentation only, explicitly stating a new policy cannot be implemented due to 'extremely limited time in the run up to LGR'.
findings.matters: Knowingly deferring complete vendor risk management during organizational change creates a material control gap at a time when operational disruption risk is highest - this is an explicit management decision to accept higher IT and supply chain risk.
findings.figures: 6 high-priority recommendations for IT Third Party Risk Management; due 31/09/2026
findings.quote: Agreed (to create guidance documentation to support staff to manage the risk rather than new policy. There is extremely limited time in the run up to LGR to effectively implement this type of new policy).

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: Network security firewall review capped at twice yearly due to understaffing
findings.detail: Internal audit recommended regular firewall rule reviews. Management partially accepted but will only conduct bi-annual reviews, explicitly citing team size constraints making more frequent reviews impossible. Audit accepted this despite acknowledging residual security risk.
findings.matters: Accepting reduced-frequency security reviews due to understaffing is a material operational risk, especially during Local Government Reorganisation when the councils face heightened change and security exposure.
findings.figures: Bi-annual (twice yearly) reviews vs. audit recommendation for regular review; due 31/01/2027
findings.quote: Partially Accepted. We will implement a bi-annual review process. Noting the team size, a more regular review is not possible.

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: Multiple critical audits received Limited assurance due to material control weaknesses
findings.detail: Internal audits issued Limited assurance opinions on Capital Programme, IT Network Security and Resilience, IT Third Party Risk Management, Adur Homes Improvement Plan, and Equalities Compliance. Limited assurance indicates the control environment is not operating effectively in these areas.
findings.matters: Limited assurance ratings on core financial and operational systems reduce the reliability of the councils' financial reporting and increase delivery risk on capital programmes - key concerns for lenders assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Capital Programme (6 recommendations, 4 medium priority); IT Network Security (5 recommendations, 1 high priority); IT Third Party Risk Management (6 recommendations, 2 high priority)
findings.quote: Final reports have been issued for Capital Programme, Commercially Leased Buildings, Adur Homes Improvement Plan, IT Network Security and Resilience, Risk Management, Corporate Governance, IT Third Party Risk Management, Key Financial Systems, and Follow Up (Part 3).

findings.paper_title: 020626 102421 - Int.Audit - A&W Progress Report - June 2026 - Final
findings.headline: Purchase orders are routinely created after invoices received, bypassing authorization controls
findings.detail: Internal audit identified that suppliers are being paid before purchase orders are formally created. Management is implementing monthly monitoring to track retrospective purchase orders and communications reminding staff of the requirement. This is a material weakness in accounts payable controls.
findings.matters: Prior authorization of spending is a fundamental control that lenders rely on to verify financial governance - when invoices trigger payment before orders exist, fraud risk increases materially and segregation of duties breaks down.
findings.figures: No threshold specified; monthly reporting to be implemented; due 31/07/2026
findings.quote: Deliver communications (or include in training as applicable) regarding the requirement for individuals to set up purchase orders following an agreed requisition and prior to initiating the purchase with suppliers.

findings.paper_title: 2026.06.16 Audit Enquiries to Those Charged With Governance
findings.headline: Worthing approved for capital flexibility of £4.75m and £5m through exceptional funding scheme for 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.detail: Worthing's budgets include approval in principle from the Minister for Housing and Local Governance to use capital flexibility through the exceptional funding scheme, allowing the council to treat capital resources as available for revenue spending. This indicates reliance on extraordinary government measures to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Use of exceptional funding schemes shows a council's ordinary revenue budget cannot balance without special government permission. This signals structural budget difficulty, not a one-off pressure.
findings.quote: In Worthing the 2025/26 and 2026/27 budgets included approval in principle from the Minister for Housing and Local Governance to use capital flexibility of up to £4.75m and £5m respectively through the exceptional funding scheme.

findings.paper_title: 2026.06.16 Audit Enquiries to Those Charged With Governance
findings.headline: Worthing has a low level of reserves and will need to liaise with MHCLG about future budget concerns
findings.detail: The Committee's proposed response identifies that while both councils face budget challenges, Adur has reserves to manage these. Worthing, however, is explicitly noted as having a low level of reserves and will liaise with MHCLG should there be concerns regarding future budgets. The 2026/27 budget includes strategies to reduce cost pressures and build reserves.
findings.matters: Low reserves reduce a council's ability to absorb budget shocks or meet unexpected costs. The need to engage MHCLG about potential future budget concerns signals anticipated financial stress.
findings.figures: None specified for reserve levels
findings.quote: Worthing has a low level of reserves however, as it did during the 2026/27 budget setting, Worthing will liaise with MHCLG should there be concerns regarding future budgets.

findings.headline: Worthing Borough Council is engaging with Government Exceptional Financial Support due to demand pressures
findings.detail: Worthing has formally engaged with Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for both 2025/26 and 2026/27 budget cycles to address demand-led budget pressures and financial stress. The council has implemented rigorous spend controls including daily reviews for items below £25,000 and weekly reviews for amounts above that threshold.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support engagement indicates a council cannot balance its budget without government intervention, representing significant financial distress
findings.figures: Daily finance reviews below £25,000; weekly Budget Management above £25,000; EFS engagement for two consecutive budget cycles
findings.quote: For both the 2025/26 and 2026/27 budget cycles, Worthing Borough Council has formally engaged with [...] demand-led pressures

findings.headline: Both councils received Limited internal audit opinions for the second consecutive year
findings.detail: Both Adur and Worthing received Limited assurance opinions from internal audit for 2024/25, continuing from the previous year. The auditors identified staff capacity issues and gaps in evidence and audit trails as recurring root causes. Three areas, including Housing Debt, were rated as Unsatisfactory.
findings.matters: A repeated Limited opinion indicates persistent governance and control weaknesses that could affect financial management and increase lending risk
findings.figures: Limited opinion for second consecutive year; three areas rated Unsatisfactory; 37% implementation rate for audit recommendations
findings.quote: In 2024/25, the Council received a 'Limited' overall opinion for the second consecutive year, with three areas [...] Housing Debt, and [...] as 'Unsatisfactory'

findings.headline: 15% of previously accepted audit recommendations remain not implemented despite tracking, indicating execution risk
findings.detail: Of 98 recommendations followed up in 2025/26, only 54% were assessed as implemented and 31% superseded, leaving 15% (15 recommendations) not implemented. While this represents a notable improvement from the prior year's 37% implementation verification rate, the fact that tracked recommendations remain incomplete suggests ongoing execution challenges.
findings.matters: Incomplete implementation of audit recommendations indicates the council may struggle to execute control improvements and remediation actions, creating ongoing governance risk.

findings.paper_title: 010626 102421 A&W - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26 - Combined DRAFT (ID 2968083)
findings.headline: Resource and capacity constraints are limiting internal audit's ability to provide assurance and management's ability to implement controls
findings.detail: The audit team explicitly identified that capacity and resourcing constraints are impacting the council's ability to produce evidence required for audit, particularly in Commercially Leased Buildings, Corporate Fire Safety, and Key Financial Systems. This includes delays in maintaining registers, lack of monitoring records, and inability to implement systems. The plan itself was not fully delivered – of 20 planned reviews, 14 were completed with 3 deferred and 3 cancelled.
findings.matters: Resource constraints limiting audit capability and hindering control implementation signal that the council may lack capacity to sustain effective financial governance and risk management going forward.
findings.figures: 14 of 20 planned reviews completed; 3 deferred, 3 cancelled; limitations noted in 'Key Financial; Procurement & Contract Management; Commercially Leased Buildings and Fire Safety'
findings.quote: Capacity / resourcing constraints impacting production of evidence required for audit (e.g. delays in maintaining registers, lack of monitoring records, incomplete updates, or inability to implement systems). This was particularly apparent in: Commercially Leased Buildings, Corporate Fire Safety, and Key Financial Systems.

findings.headline: Capital Programme audit produced Limited assurance opinion with 4 Medium and 2 Low priority recommendations
findings.detail: The Capital Programme review, a key financial control area, received a Limited assurance opinion (15 days actual audit). The council received 4 Medium priority and 2 Low priority recommendations across this area, indicating significant control weaknesses in capital scheme governance and oversight.
findings.matters: Weaknesses in capital programme controls affect the council's ability to deliver and monitor major investment schemes, relevant to infrastructure planning and borrowing decisions.

findings.detail: High priority recommendations (defined as significant weaknesses exposing the organisation to unacceptable residual risk) were raised across six reviews: Leisure Contract Health & Safety, Equalities Act Compliance, Corporate Fire Safety, Procurement/Contract Management, IT Third Party Risk Management, and IT Network Security and Resilience. These represent weaknesses that require urgent remedial action.
findings.matters: Unresolved High priority audit findings indicate material control weaknesses in critical areas – particularly capital investment, procurement, IT systems and contractual risk – that increase financial and operational risk.

findings.quote: High Priority recommendations were raised in six reviews (Leisure Contract -Health & Safety, Equalities Act Compliance, Corporate Fire Safety, Procurement / Contract Management, IT Third Party Risk Management, IT Network Security and Resilience).

findings.paper_title: 010626 102421 A&W - Internal Audit Annual Report 2025-26 - Combined DRAFT (ID 2968083)
findings.headline: Annual internal audit opinion is Limited – significant weaknesses in governance, risk management and control that could become inadequate and ineffective
findings.detail: The council received a Limited assurance opinion, unchanged from the prior year (2024/25). This means there are significant weaknesses in the framework of governance, risk management and control such that it could be or could become inadequate and ineffective. Of 12 assurance reviews, 8 provided Limited opinions and only 4 provided Moderate assurance.
findings.matters: A Limited assurance opinion signals material gaps in the control environment that a lender would need to factor into credit risk assessment and monitoring.
findings.figures: 8 of 12 assurance reviews provided Limited opinions; 4 provided Moderate assurance
findings.quote: our opinion on the framework of governance, risk management, and control is Limited in its overall adequacy and effectiveness. As such, there are significant weaknesses in the framework of governance, risk management and control such that it could be or could become inadequate and ineffective.

findings.headline: The council faces sustained financial pressure from housing demand and growth in supported accommodation within the borough.
findings.detail: The council has faced increasing costs from growing housing demand and supported accommodation since 2022/23. This has contributed directly to the need for exceptional financial support. While the council has absorbed pressure from sector-wide austerity, these local demand pressures appear structural rather than cyclical.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures that drive budget deficits are more worrying than cyclical pressures. If supported accommodation and housing are growing faster than council capacity or grant funding, the underlying financial problem may deteriorate rather than improve, making future EFS applications likely.
findings.figures: £4.75 million EFS needed in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council has faced sustained financial pressures arising from increased housing demand and the growth of supported accommodation within the Borough since 2022/23.

findings.headline: Investment property valuations have been materially misstated in the prior year and remain a significant audit risk.
findings.detail: The auditors have identified the valuation of investment properties under fair value as a 'significant risk' with 'continued material misstatements identified in 2024/25'. The valuations rely heavily on the council's external valuer and management's judgements about yields and assumptions. The auditors plan to involve their own real estate specialists to challenge the valuations.
findings.matters: Material misstatements in valuations of a major asset class (investment properties represent significant balance sheet figures) indicate either weak controls over the valuation process or management bias in accounting estimates. This is a control weakness that affects the reliability of the financial statements.
findings.figures: Investment properties represent material figures in the financial statements; Property, Plant & Equipment £222.31 million at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The valuation of IP remains a significant risk due to the continued material misstatements identified in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Internal audit has issued a Limited Assurance opinion for two consecutive years, with multiple control areas rated as unsatisfactory or limited.
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit issued Limited Assurance opinions in both 2023/24 and 2024/25. In 2024/25, of 22 audit reviews, 7 received Limited Assurance ratings and 3 received Unsatisfactory Assurance ratings. The auditors have flagged this as a 'risk of significant weakness' in governance for 2025/26 and recommend that those charged with governance hold officers accountable for completing the action plan to address these deficiencies.
findings.matters: Persistent internal control weaknesses across multiple areas signal systemic governance failures. Two consecutive limited assurance opinions indicate the council has not resolved control deficiencies, which increases the risk of undetected error or loss in financial reporting and service delivery.
findings.figures: 7 out of 22 reviews Limited Assurance; 3 out of 22 Unsatisfactory; 4 out of 22 Moderate
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit (HoIA) issued a Limited Assurance Opinion in both 2023/24 and 2024/25, indicating persistent weaknesses in the effectiveness of the Council's internal control framework. The HoIA Annual Report for 2024/25 reported that, out of 22 audit and advisory reviews undertaken during the year, seven received Limited Assurance and three received Unsatisfactory Assurance ratings, with a further four reviews assessed as Moderate Assurance.

findings.headline: The council's reserves are unreliably stated because audit opinions have been disclaimed for two consecutive years.
findings.detail: The auditors issued disclaimed opinions in both 2024/25 and 2023/24, meaning they could not form an opinion on the financial statements as a whole. The 2025/26 plan includes a 'historic rebuild' of assurance, including auditing transactions from 2022/23, because gaps in evidence over usable and unusable reserves have not been resolved. Management must complete a detailed review and reconciliation of reserves before audit procedures can commence.
findings.matters: If the council's reserves cannot be reliably stated, its true financial position is unknown. Lenders cannot assess financial cushion or covenant compliance. The council and auditors are attempting a multi-year rebuild, which suggests the underlying problem is fundamental, not routine.
findings.figures: Pension liability at 31 March 2025 was £14.14 million; Property, Plant & Equipment balance £222.31 million (with £139.24 million in land and buildings); audit materiality set at £1.64 million
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a disclaimed audit opinion was issued. While we had completed all planned procedures, the gaps in audit assurance over the classification of the Council's reserves, deriving from the disclaimers in prior years was judged to be fundamental to users of the accounts given Worthing BC's financial position.

findings.headline: The council cannot balance its budget without government support and will continue to rely on it in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Worthing BC needed £4.75 million in Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from central government to achieve a balanced budget for 2025/26. The auditors have identified the council's ongoing reliance on EFS as a 'risk of significant weakness' in financial sustainability for 2025/26, and the continued application for EFS in 2026/27 budget planning is listed as a continuing concern.
findings.matters: A council dependent on annual emergency funding to balance the books has no margin for deterioration and represents heightened credit risk; lenders need to know whether the underlying pressures (housing and supported accommodation) are structural or temporary.
findings.figures: £4.75 million EFS for 2025/26; 2024/25 gross expenditure £82.04 million
findings.quote: As a result, it has applied to the MHCLG for £4.75 million in EFS to achieve a balanced budget for 2025/26. Therefore, the Council's reserves were insufficient to absorb the projected revenue overspend, indicating that the 2025/26 budget was not soundly based on a value for money perspective.

findings.headline: Finance team requires training and capacity support; audit dependent on management responsiveness and resource allocation
findings.detail: The auditors have planned a training workshop for June 2026 to support the finance team's readiness for 2025/26 financial statement preparation. The audit report explicitly states that the audit's ability to complete is dependent on management allocating sufficient knowledgeable resources, timely provision of working papers, and management's responsiveness to audit issues. Prior assessments show these areas need improvement.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity and capability directly affect the quality of financial reporting and audit efficiency. Inadequate resourcing or skill gaps increase the risk of errors in accounts preparation and may signal resource constraints limiting the council's ability to manage its finances effectively.
findings.figures: Training workshop scheduled for June 2026
findings.quote: To support the finance team's readiness for the preparation of the 2025/26 financial statements, and to assist in improving the delivery of working papers in accordance with the agreed schedule, the quality of working papers and supporting evidence, and the timeliness and quality of evidence supporting key accounting estimates, we agreed and planned a scheduled training workshop in June 2026.

findings.headline: New audit risk: Adur Homes cut-off errors in prior year; risk of misstatement in repairs/maintenance and capital additions
findings.detail: Based on errors identified in 2024/25, a new risk has been flagged for 2025/26 relating to accounting cut-off for Adur Homes Housing Revenue Account repairs/maintenance and council dwelling additions. The quality and completeness of information from the Adur Homes team made it difficult for the finance team to determine correct accounting treatment, resulting in prior-year errors.
findings.matters: Cut-off errors can result in material misstatements of expenditure and capital balances, affecting both revenue and capital accounts. This signals ongoing data quality issues between Adur Homes and the finance team, creating audit and control risk.
findings.figures: Errors identified in 2024/25 relating to cut-off
findings.quote: Based on the errors identified in the 2024/25 financial year, we have identified a Risk of Material Misstatement relating to cut-off for Adur Homes Housing Revenue Account (HRA) repairs and maintenance expenditure, and council dwelling additions. The quality and completeness of information provided by the Adur Homes team has made it difficult for Finance team to determine the correct accounting cut-off.

findings.headline: Adur Homes housing stock continues to have significant non-compliance with Housing Standards; fourth consecutive year of reported weakness
findings.detail: The audit has reported non-compliance with relevant Housing Standards in connection with Adur Homes' housing stock for four consecutive financial periods. This matter remains a risk of significant weakness in 2025/26. The council is operating a Housing Improvement Plan to address these governance and compliance issues within Adur Homes.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with housing standards exposes the council to reputational, legal, and financial risk. It suggests governance weaknesses over a major asset (housing stock) and service delivery function, affecting both borrowing risk and service quality to residents.
findings.figures: Four consecutive financial periods with reported non-compliance
findings.quote: We have previously reported a significant weakness in each of the preceding four financial periods relating to non-compliance with relevant Housing Standards in connection with Adur Homes' housing stock. This matter to continues to represent a risk of significant weakness in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Internal audit issued limited assurance opinions in both 2023/24 and 2024/25, with 7 of 22 reviews rated Limited Assurance and 3 rated Unsatisfactory
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit (HoIA) has issued Limited Assurance Opinions for two consecutive years (2023/24 and 2024/25). Of 22 audit and advisory reviews undertaken in 2024/25, seven received Limited Assurance ratings and three received Unsatisfactory Assurance ratings, with only four rated Moderate Assurance. This distribution indicates pervasive and persistent control weaknesses across key council operations.
findings.matters: Consecutive limited assurance opinions from internal audit signal systemic control deficiencies that increase risk of errors, fraud, or mismanagement. This is a value-for-money risk and governance concern that affects the council's ability to manage resources effectively.
findings.figures: 22 audit reviews: 7 Limited Assurance, 3 Unsatisfactory, 4 Moderate; Limited Assurance opinion issued in 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.quote: The Head of Internal Audit (HoIA) issued a Limited Assurance Opinion in both 2023/24 and 2024/25, indicating persistent weaknesses in the effectiveness of the Council's internal control framework. The HoIA Annual Report for 2024/25 reported that, out of 22 audit and advisory reviews undertaken during the year, seven received Limited Assurance and three received Unsatisfactory Assurance ratings.

findings.headline: Investment property valuations carried material misstatements in 2024/25; significant risk continues
findings.detail: Investment property valuations represent material figures in the balance sheet and were subject to material misstatements in the prior year. The audit flagged this as a significant risk for 2025/26 specifically because errors have already been found. Valuations depend heavily on the council's external valuer and the information and judgments provided to them.
findings.matters: Material misstatements in asset valuations directly affect the balance sheet and can inflate asset values, distorting the council's true financial position. This is especially important for councils holding investment property as part of their revenue strategy.
findings.figures: Investment properties are material figures in the balance sheet
findings.quote: The valuation of IP remains a significant risk due to the continued material misstatements identified in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion in 2024/25 following disclaimer in 2023/24; multi-year rebuild of assurance still underway
findings.detail: The council received a qualified audit opinion for 2024/25 (after a disclaimer in 2023/24) due to prior-year evidence gaps. The audit team is now undertaking a phased rebuild to move from qualified to unqualified opinions, starting with completion of all planned procedures and moving toward rebuilding assurance over historic balances including reserves. This reflects material weaknesses in financial reporting and control environment that took effect over multiple years.
findings.matters: Qualification or disclaimer of audit opinions directly affects creditworthiness assessments and signals material deficiencies in accounting controls and financial statement reliability. Lenders need confidence in audited figures; a qualified opinion is a red flag.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinion 2023/24; Qualified opinion 2024/25; recovery expected to take multiple years
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2024 disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the application of the backstop. In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a qualified audit opinion was issued which drew attention to remaining limitations in audit evidence arising from prior-year disclaimers of opinion.

findings.headline: Treasury costs remain under pressure from sustained high interest rates and delays in property disposals.
findings.detail: Worthing forecasts a £35k overspend in treasury management due to sustained period of increased interest rates and delays in property disposals. While some mitigation measures are in place per the treasury management strategy, the report notes that future rates and completion of asset sales remain uncertain risks. Falling interest rates are expected to harm short-term investment income for the remainder of the financial year.
findings.matters: Interest rate pressure on treasury costs signals that the council has significant debt or property holdings exposed to rate movements. In a higher-for-longer interest rate environment, this cost will not disappear. For a lender, this indicates the council's existing debt service costs are consuming operational income.
findings.figures: £35k treasury overspend in Worthing; sustained period of increased interest rates; delays in property disposals impacting forecast; risk of further pressure from ECB, MPC, and US Fed rate decisions
findings.quote: Treasury budgets continue to be pressured by a sustained period of increased interest rates and delays in property disposals, though a number of mitigation measures are in place

findings.headline: Worthing received £2m in Exceptional Funding Support from MHCLG for 2025/26 but is still in deficit and seeking additional support.
findings.detail: Worthing already received £2m in exceptional funding support for 2025/26 via the government's Exceptional Funding Support scheme. Despite this, the council is still forecasting an overspend and is in ongoing discussions with MHCLG regarding additional financial pressures and support. The report notes that MHCLG has been informed the council "currently anticipates requiring additional funding support to mitigate the projected overspend, as there are insufficient reserve balances to cover this shortfall."
findings.matters: A council already receiving exceptional government support and still facing deficit indicates structural, not cyclical, fiscal stress. The fact that £2m of exceptional money only partially addresses the problem and reserves remain depleted signals the underlying issues (homelessness, income shortfalls) are beyond the council's control or current spending plan to fix. Future support is uncertain.
findings.figures: £2m Exceptional Funding Support received for 2025/26; forecast overspend after support £3.733m (originally £5.733m before support); council seeking additional support beyond initial allocation
findings.quote: MHCLG has been informed that the Council currently anticipates requiring additional funding support to mitigate the projected overspend, as there are insufficient reserve balances to cover this shortfall.

findings.headline: Adur Housing Revenue Account overspend of £366k driven by void losses (£734k) despite efforts to manage costs.
findings.detail: The Adur HRA is forecast to overspend by £366k. Void property rent loss totals £734k adverse variance (including associated service charge losses and increased Council Tax liabilities from extended void periods). This is despite staff cost savings of £522k from reallocation to capital projects. The HRA General Reserve will fall from budgeted £1.38m to forecast £1.01m (9% of gross expenditure, within but at lower end of policy range).
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced but still part of the council's overall financial position. Void losses in council housing indicate maintenance, lettings, or market problems. While staffing savings helped this year, the underlying void issue (properties not letting as expected) is not solved and will recur.
findings.figures: £366k HRA overspend; £734k void rent loss; £522k staff cost savings (time allocated to capital); General Reserve forecast £1.01m (down from £1.38m budgeted)
findings.quote: The HRA is forecast to over spend against the budget for 2025/26 by £366k. The most significant variances are due to: Void property rent loss (including losses in associated service charges and increased Council Tax liabilities) - £734k adverse.

findings.headline: Strategic property investments are underperforming: Worthing Integrated Care Centre opening delayed, causing £346k rental income loss.
findings.detail: Worthing's planned transfer to the Property Investment Risk Reserve (£750k budgeted) will not be made in 2025/26 due to property portfolio underperformance. The Worthing Integrated Care Centre has not yet opened, creating a £346k rental income shortfall. The Beta building has been sold, reducing ongoing rental income by £379k. Additional void properties elsewhere in the portfolio are unlet.
findings.matters: Investment property income is supposed to be more stable than demand-led services. Delays in opening a major facility and asset sales suggest capital plans are behind schedule. This impacts cash flow forecasting and, for a council managing significant property assets, signals execution risk on capital projects that are relied upon for income.
findings.figures: £346k shortfall from delayed WICC opening; £379k income loss from Beta building sale; planned reserve transfer of £750k not being made; additional void losses in strategic portfolio
findings.quote: This is mainly due to the Worthing Integrated Community Centre not being opened, with a rental shortfall of £346K expected. Additionally, one of the assets has now been sold, thus creating an income rental shortfall of £379K.

findings.headline: Bereavement services (crematorium and cemetery) are down £676k in Worthing—a demand-led income stream in decline.
findings.detail: Worthing crematorium faces a £759k shortfall driven by lower death rates and competition from funeral directors' own facilities and cheaper direct cremation options. The budget was already reset downward by £500k in 2024/25 but shortfalls persist. This is not a temporary issue: it reflects underlying demographic and market trends. Cemetery income is slightly ahead but cannot offset cremation losses.
findings.matters: A council income stream is only reliable if demand is stable or growing. Bereavement services demonstrate a declining and price-sensitive market. The fact the budget was cut once and still underperforms suggests forecasts are not calibrated to reality. For lenders, this shows an income base eroding due to factors beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: £676k net deficit in Worthing bereavement services; crematorium forecast shortfall £759k; previous budget reset of £500k in 2024/25 did not eliminate variance; death rates lower than anticipated nationally
findings.quote: The bereavement service continues to deliver a net surplus, but faces a £675,990 deficit against its budget target in Worthing. Despite a budget reset for 24/25 that reduced income targets by £500k following a commercial review, a shortfall persists.

findings.headline: Worthing car park income is down £899k due to structural post-pandemic demand collapse and Grafton multi-storey closure.
findings.detail: Parking income shortfall of £899k comprises £638k in lost income and £261k in maintenance/security costs. The Grafton Multi-Storey car park closed on 16 May 2025 for safety reasons, eliminating £677k of income. The underlying issue is structural: parking demand has not recovered to pre-pandemic levels and remote working has permanently reduced commuter parking. The report notes this is beyond tariff increases or service redesign to fix—it reflects changed working patterns.
findings.matters: Income volatility is concerning for debt serviceability. When car parks are relied upon as a council income source and demand has structurally declined, the council cannot raise that income through efficiency alone. This is a demand shock, not a management failure. It signals that other council incomes (planning fees, bereavement services) similarly at risk from structural market changes.
findings.figures: £899k shortfall (11.4% of parking budget); £677k loss from Grafton closure; £638k income shortfall; £261k in ongoing maintenance and security costs for closed facility
findings.quote: Worthing Car Parks are currently forecasting a net underachievement of budget of £899k due to a combination of drop in demand (which has not recovered since the pandemic), car park closures (both permanent and temporary) and the delayed tariff increases

findings.headline: Exempt Supported Accommodation in Worthing has exploded 221% since 2021, creating £800k annual Housing Benefit subsidy loss.
findings.detail: Non-registered supported accommodation providers operate under housing benefit rules that cap council reimbursement at 2011 Local Housing Allowance rates, regardless of actual rental costs. Worthing has seen 221% growth in units since 2021. The council cannot claim full Housing Benefit subsidy back on these properties—the value of unrecoverable costs in 2025/26 is forecast at £800k. The Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 enables oversight but won't address cost pressures until 2027/28.
findings.matters: This is a housing market failure that directly hits the council's budget. Supply constraints and housing costs force vulnerable people into expensive supported accommodation, but outdated subsidy caps haven't been updated in over a decade. The council cannot refuse the cost: it must house people or break statutory law. This is a durable fiscal pressure independent of council performance.
findings.figures: 221% increase in units in Worthing since 2021; £800k projected unrecoverable Housing Benefit subsidy in Worthing for 2025/26; £128k in Adur; unregistered providers restrict subsidy claims to Market Rent ceiling
findings.quote: These providers operate under specific financial rules that differ from standard housing arrangements... Councils are therefore restricted in the amount of subsidy that can be claimed back on these properties up to the Market Rent (which is based on 2011 levels).

findings.headline: Worthing's homelessness service is overspending by £3.159m—more than double the council's entire overspend.
findings.detail: Housing Needs costs in Worthing are forecast to exceed budget by £3.159m due to high caseloads in temporary accommodation, limited move-on options, and void costs running 6.1% against a 5% target. New homelessness approaches in Worthing stood at 503 by end of Q3, representing ongoing pressure. The service is statutorily obliged to provide accommodation, limiting the council's ability to control spending.
findings.matters: Statutory homelessness duties cannot be cut without legal risk. A lender assessing loan sustainability must account for this cost as essentially fixed regardless of the council's other financial performance. The fact it consumes 85% of total overspend shows where the real fiscal pressure sits.
findings.figures: £3.159m overspend in Worthing housing needs; 503 new homelessness approaches by Q3 2025/26 (up from 480 in Q3 2024/25); 6.1% actual void rate vs 5% budgeted; temporary accommodation average cost £13,476 per placement
findings.quote: Cost pressures continue to persist in discharging our statutory duties due to the steady number of cases involving individuals, couples, and families presenting to the council as homeless.

findings.headline: Worthing Borough Council faces £3.733m overspend that will exhaust all available reserves.
findings.detail: The forecast outturn is an overspend of £3.733m after government funding and reserve transfers. Available reserves total only £1.58m but the overspend requires £1.81m in drawdown, creating a projected shortfall of £302k. The council's General Fund Working Balance policy targets 6-10% of net revenue expenditure but reserves will be fully utilised with nothing left for contingency.
findings.matters: A local authority with zero financial reserves cannot absorb unexpected shocks and signals to lenders that the council is at the limits of fiscal sustainability. This determines borrowing capacity and repayment confidence.
findings.figures: £3.733m overspend; £1.58m available reserves; projected £302k shortfall after overspend; General Fund Working Balance currently £755k (4.2% of net expenditure, below the 6% floor)
findings.quote: the total reserves figure would be fully utilised and there would be a shortfall of £302,286

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: Capital budget for new SPIF investment has been cut in recent reviews and further acquisitions will require specific approval and business cases.
findings.detail: Section 18.3: 'The Councils approved an overall investment of £125m per Council, however following capital programme reviews the available budget has been reduced. This does not preclude the councils from making such investments in the future, however they will need to be considered through full governance in order to make the capital budget available.' This indicates funding pressure and governance hurdles that slow investment decisions.
findings.matters: Reduced capital availability constrains the council's ability to manage portfolio risks (refresh aging assets, address MEES issues, rebalance sector exposure). It signals budget pressure and may indicate the council is drawing down reserves or delaying necessary capex.
findings.figures: Approved £125m per council; available budget reduced; £850k–£750k annual maintenance provision (Adur/Worthing)
findings.quote: The Councils approved an overall investment of £125m per Council, however following capital programme reviews the available budget has been reduced.

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing costs have risen sharply and new lending restrictions have made the investment model significantly less viable than when funds were first created.
findings.detail: Section 3.3 notes 'PWLB rates have ranged from below 1% to in excess of 6% during the last decade', and rates post-2022 are 'less favourable than borrowing prior to 2022'. Section 3.4: 'Revised 2021 onward PWLB Funding arrangements resulted in increased scrutiny on borrowing, preventing the use of this loan facility to fund new investments primarily for yield.' The original strategy assumed higher spread between yield and borrowing costs; this is no longer available.
findings.matters: The financial model that justified the £250m investment is broken. Higher rates mean the margin between rental income and debt servicing cost has eroded. This threatens the sustainability of income contributions and creates pressure to dispose of lower-performing assets.
findings.figures: PWLB rates 1% to 6%+ over past decade; current rates above cost assumptions in original strategy
findings.quote: The Councils' cost of borrowing from the PWLB and other sources has become less favourable than borrowing prior to 2022. PWLB rates have ranged from below 1% to in excess of 6% during the last decade.

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: The portfolio is heavily weighted to office properties in a sector experiencing structural decline, with weak demand for secondary space.
findings.detail: Both councils' SPIF portfolios are 'weighted towards office investments'. Market commentary (section 7) acknowledges that 'secondary office stock [is] being repurposed or demolished where they face economic and physical obsolescence'. Nationally, 'reluctance...to return to the workplace full time, and digitisation and improved remote working have changed the requirements of office tenants, which in turn drives obsolescence risks and so this sector is still experiencing disruption'. The paper notes demand for office space 'remains very thin in our Borough and District areas'.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council's income assumptions are realistic. The council admits its portfolio is exposed to a declining sector facing structural headwinds, yet cannot diversify due to geographic constraints and lack of available stock.
findings.figures: Office properties form the largest weighting; portfolio includes alternatives (hotel, car parking, gym, lab) but office dominates capital allocation
findings.quote: Nationally, the very best office space is sought after, the less attractive or well-located spaces, with doubtful energy performance certification and amenities, are much less in demand, if in demand at all...secondary office stock being repurposed or demolished where they face economic and physical obsolescence.

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: New investment has stopped for over three years and the council expects no material new acquisitions in 2026 due to PWLB lending rules and lack of suitable local stock.
findings.detail: The last acquisition was November 2022. Section 8.8 states: 'During 2026 officers do not expect to be inundated with opportunities that meet these CPIS criteria within our Council areas.' PWLB 2021 rules 'prevented the use of this loan facility to fund new investments primarily for yield', and the council's geographic restriction (properties must be in Adur district only) has created a 'lack of Grade A investment property in our areas'. Portfolio 'is very unlikely to change materially its component parts, other than by disposals'.
findings.matters: Portfolio stagnation compounds income risk. An aging portfolio cannot refresh tenant mix or upgrade assets except through defensive capex. The council is trapped: unable to grow income, forced to spend on compliance, and locked into existing tenant relationships.
findings.figures: 0 acquisitions in ~3 years; £125m approved but available budget 'has been reduced' post-review
findings.quote: During the last financial year, no new purchases were made, the last being in November 2022...During 2026 officers do not expect to be inundated with opportunities that meet these CPIS criteria within our Council areas.

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: The council faces mandatory capital spending of millions on energy efficiency compliance by 2030 to keep properties lettable.
findings.detail: From 2030, the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) will require a minimum EPC rating of A/B/C across all let properties. The council has 'identified shortfalls' and is 'planning to address this through a revised capital programme'. Failure to comply means properties cannot legally be let. This creates a hard deadline for capex that will reduce available income and increase maintenance costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to forecast the council's debt servicing capacity through 2030. The energy compliance bill is a known, legally-mandated liability that the council has not yet fully quantified or budgeted.
findings.figures: A/B/C EPC threshold mandatory by 2030; existing maintenance budget £850k (Adur) annually, described as inadequate
findings.quote: There will be a minimum Energy Performance Certificate threshold of A/B/C in 2030 beyond which it will be illegal to let space at a lower grade. Officers have identified shortfalls and are planning to address this through a revised capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: Three tenants have failed and two payments have turned into bad debts, with retail and hospitality tenants flagged as ongoing concerns.
findings.detail: The portfolio has experienced tenant failures including 'a household name' and 'two of the smaller tenants'. During 2025, rent collection was 97%, but 'two of those late payments turning into bad debts through tenant liquidation'. Retail and hospitality sectors 'remain a concern and are being monitored'. These are material income risks.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the portfolio's cashflow reliability must account for tenant covenant deterioration. A 97% collection rate with ongoing bad debts suggests mounting tenant stress, particularly in vulnerable sectors.
findings.figures: Rent collection 97%; 2 tenants liquidated; 3 total tenant failures
findings.quote: However two of the smaller tenants have failed, as has a household name, and others especially in retail and hospitality, remain a concern and are being monitored.

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026_27 (1)
findings.headline: The council's budget strategy depends critically on commercial property income to offset central government cuts and a deficit position.
findings.detail: SPIF rental income makes up 64% of Adur's total non-residential property income. The investment strategy is explicitly described as 'significantly affected by the Council's deficit position', and section 16 notes that without this income, the council would have faced 'an overall reduction in the capacity of the Councils to deliver, with cuts in services'. The income 'contributes to the budget as the Councils continue to address significant financial challenges'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can sustain this income stream. If the portfolio falters, the entire budget strategy falls apart, and the council has no alternative revenue source to cover the shortfall.
findings.figures: 64% of non-residential property income; £125m per council fund size
findings.quote: The investment strategy is significantly affected by the Council's deficit position so in 2025 officers re-focused their efforts on rent collection and tenant engagement, to preserve the Council's revenue position.

findings.headline: Food waste service implementation costs £540k in 2026/27 with ongoing £560k-£610k annual costs through 2030/31
findings.detail: The council is introducing a new food waste service at a cost of £540k in 2026/27 with committed ongoing costs growing to £610k by 2030/31. This is a permanent addition to the cost base driven by extended producer responsibility legislation and cannot be reversed.
findings.matters: New statutory service costs reduce headroom further and are permanent, adding to the structural deficit challenge.
findings.quote: Implementation of food waste service

findings.headline: Council tax increase of 2.99% needed to achieve balanced budget; lower increases would require reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The budget assumes 2.99% council tax increase to deliver a balanced budget for 2026/27. Any lower increase (1%, 1.5%, 2%) would create a budget shortfall requiring drawdown of the already-tight General Fund Working Balance. With deficits forecast from 2027/28, relying on reserves to plug council tax decisions is unsustainable.
findings.matters: The council has no margin to absorb a decision to hold or reduce council tax increases. Any political pressure to constrain council tax growth will force immediate reserve depletion.
findings.figures: 2.99% increase needed for balance; 1% increase would reduce income by £155k versus planned 2.99%
findings.quote: The Executive will need to consider whether to increase council tax by 2.99% or by a lower amount

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset eliminates £9m accumulated retained growth and introduces declining safety net protection from 2027/28
findings.detail: The business rates retention scheme, unchanged since 2013, has been fundamentally reset. The accumulated national growth (estimated over £1.5bn nationally) is being reclaimed by government. Adur loses its retained growth and moves to baseline funding of £2.05m. Safety net protection is 100% in 2026/27 but steps down to 97.5% (2027/28) and 92.5% (2028/29), creating downside risk.
findings.matters: The reset wipes out historical growth accumulated by the council and introduces future volatility as safety net protection decreases, creating downside risk to a volatile income stream.
findings.figures: Accumulated growth approximately £9m reset; Baseline funding £2.050m (2026/27), £2.034m (2027/28), £1.979m (2028/29); Safety net at 100%, 97.5%, 92.5%
findings.quote: The government has fundamentally redesigned the Business Rates Levy structure.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £276k carried forward and recovered from 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council has a Collection Fund deficit at the end of the current year, partially due to business rate reliefs granted in prior years. This deficit of £276k must be recovered in 2026/27, adding to budget pressures and reducing flexibility.
findings.matters: Collection deficits indicate prior-year income shortfalls and create additional pressure on current budgets, leaving no headroom for further income volatility.
findings.figures: £276k Collection Fund deficit to be recovered in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Collection Fund will have another deficit at the end of the current year

findings.headline: Housing cost pressures driven by temporary accommodation demand rising £300k in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council is making a £300k growth bid for increased housing budget costs due to temporary accommodation demand, plus a further £120k investment in housing prevention. The multi-year forecast shows continued £300k-£100k annual growth in housing costs through 2030/31.
findings.matters: Rising temporary accommodation costs indicate deteriorating housing conditions and social pressures in the district that are draining council finances and likely to persist.
findings.figures: £300k additional growth for temporary accommodation; £120k for housing prevention; ongoing £200k-£100k annual growth forecast through 2030/31
findings.quote: Increased costs associated with temporary accommodation

findings.headline: Material dependence on commercial property investment income at £4.66m annually, approximately 35% of council's own-source income
findings.detail: The council generates £4.66m annually from strategic property investment funds. This income is material to budget sustainability and the council is planning further investment. However, the budget notes ongoing uncertainties around borrowing costs and property values.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is volatile and subject to market conditions, void periods, and borrowing cost swings. Over-reliance creates exposure if property markets weaken or interest rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: £4.66m annual income from strategic property investment portfolio, with further investment planned
findings.quote: the strategic property investment funds generated income of £4.66m in

findings.headline: Income from fees and charges underperforming budget, with council relying on 2% fee increases to bridge shortfalls
findings.detail: The budget notes that current year forecasts show performance shortfalls against budgeted income due to less income growth than expected. Rather than increasing budgets, the council has assumed 2% average increases in fees and charges portfolio-wide will mitigate these shortfalls. This creates risk: if uptake or volumes fall further, the council will be forced to draw reserves or cut services mid-year.
findings.matters: If income shortfalls persist or deteriorate further, the council will have no buffer and will be forced to draw reserves or cut services, neither sustainable in a growing deficit environment.
findings.figures: Assumed 2% average increase in fees and charges assumed to mitigate current-year performance shortfalls; actual shortfall amounts not separately disclosed
findings.quote: the current year forecasts project a number of performance shortfalls against budget due

findings.headline: General Fund Working Balance at 9.8% of budget, described by officers as 'low'
findings.detail: The council maintains a General Fund Working Balance of £1.1m at 9.8% of budget, within the stated policy range of 6-10%, but officers explicitly describe it as 'currently projected to be low at year end'. The council plans to build this to £1.3m by 2027, but any in-year pressure or funding change would erode flexibility.
findings.matters: Low reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb external shocks or funding changes, increasing reliance on borrowing or immediate service cuts.
findings.figures: Current General Fund Working Balance £1.1m (9.8% of budget), target to increase to £1.3m (9.7%) by March 2027
findings.quote: The working balance is currently projected to be low at year end.

findings.headline: Growing structural deficits from 2027/28 requiring savings of £134k rising to £2.5m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial plan shows a balanced budget for 2026/27, but cumulative shortfalls grow from £134k in 2027/28 to £2,545k by 2030/31. The budget does not identify how these shortfalls will be funded, indicating reliance on future savings, service cuts, or further council tax rises.
findings.matters: Growing deficits signal structural financial imbalance requiring material service reductions or unsustainable council tax increases, a key credit risk.
findings.quote: Amount required to balance the budget    0  134  510  1,709  2,545

findings.headline: Council proposing £540,000 recurring growth for new food waste collection service
findings.detail: The council is launching weekly food waste collections in September at a cost of £540,000, with ten new vehicles on order. This represents a new fixed cost locked into the base budget.
findings.matters: New service commitments reduce budget flexibility and make future savings harder to achieve. The council is adding cost at a time when it is already under pressure.
findings.figures: £540,000 growth for food waste services; 10 new vehicles on order
findings.quote: We'll launch weekly food waste collections in September. We have ten new vehicles on order for this.

findings.headline: Council leadership signals local government still faces material financial risk despite nominal budget balance
findings.detail: Whilst the 2026/27 budget is balanced with contributions to reserves, the council leader explicitly cautions that 'local government is not out of the woods' and warns the council faces 'challenges compounded by the uncertainty and complexity of local government reorganisation'.
findings.matters: The council's own assessment of ongoing distress and structural uncertainty (LG reorganisation) undermines confidence in medium-term stability, even if this year balances.
findings.figures: Council tax increase 2.99%; balance achieved with reserve contributions
findings.quote: we must not underestimate the fact that local government is not out of the woods, our council faces challenges compounded by the uncertainty and complexity of local government reorganisation.

findings.headline: Albion Street council housing project slipped again; remedial work estimated at two months
findings.detail: The 49-unit new build at Albion Street has experienced ongoing delays due to construction problems. Scaffolding has been re-erected and remedial work is estimated to take two months before residents can move in. The council apologises for the 'dreadful' delays.
findings.matters: Repeated capital project delays suggest weak project governance or contractor issues. This affects housing delivery targets and raises questions about the council's ability to manage its capital programme.
findings.figures: 49 council homes; remedial work estimated at two months
findings.quote: The saga of Albion Street continues with scaffolding up again around this building so that problems can be rectified before people move in. Thorough investigations have taken place and the work getting underway is estimated to last two months.

findings.headline: £4m savings programme complete but leaving services with capacity challenges and staff pressure
findings.detail: The council completed a significant redesign programme delivering over £4m in savings. However, the speech explicitly acknowledges this has left some services with capacity challenges and pressure on staff, indicating the savings were achieved through workforce reductions that may now constrain service delivery.
findings.matters: Deep cuts can impair the council's ability to collect income, manage risk, and respond to demand. Services run thin are at risk of failure when unexpected costs arise.
findings.figures: £4m in savings from redesign programme
findings.quote: This council has, of course, undergone a significant redesign programme delivering savings of more than £4m. Savings that were essential but leave some of our services with capacity challenges; pressure on staff.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation now consumes 16% of Adur's budget
findings.detail: The council identifies homelessness funding as a significant financial pressure. At November 2025 there were 161 households in temporary accommodation. Whilst the council notes a reduction in placements between January 2025 and January 2026, it is proposing growth spending of £300,000 for temporary accommodation services and £120,000 for homelessness prevention.
findings.matters: A budget line consuming 16% and still growing signals unsustainable cost dynamics that could create future deficits. Lenders need confidence this trend can be arrested.
findings.figures: 16% of budget on temporary accommodation; 161 households in temporary accommodation (November 2025); £300,000 new growth for temporary accommodation; £120,000 for prevention
findings.quote: The cost of funding temporary accommodation for Adur residents now takes up 16% of our budget.

findings.headline: Council approved using capital receipts to fund Local Government Reorganisation transition costs
findings.detail: The council is using capital receipts—finite, one-off resources—to fund transformation costs from the Organisational Design Programme and transition work for Local Government Reorganisation. Specific amounts and timeline are in appendices not provided in this extract.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale and timeline of capital receipts usage for reorganisation and whether the council will maintain adequate reserves for financial stability during the transition
findings.figures: Amounts not specified in this extract; detail in section 6.2 and appendix 4
findings.quote: That the use of Capital receipts be approved to support a) Residual transformation costs associated with the Organisational Design Programme, and b) Transition work required for the Local Government Reorganisation (detail set out in section 6.2 and appendix 4

findings.headline: Council tax income increases not built into 2026/27 budget despite inflation because current-year fees and charges are underperforming
findings.detail: The councils state that 'Income growth from the proposed inflationary increases to fees and charges have not been built into the 2026/27 budgets. The decision recognises that in the current financial year there are a number of income lines forecast to fall below the target budget.' This means they are assuming flat income despite inflation, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Income lines that are systematically underperforming against budget indicate either overly optimistic budgeting or deteriorating service demand or competitiveness.
findings.figures: Current-year income forecast to fall below target budget by unspecified amount; no fees/charges growth assumption built in
findings.quote: Income growth from the proposed inflationary increases to fees and charges have not been built into the 2026/27 budgets. The decision recognises that in the current financial year there are a number of income lines forecast to fall below the target budget

findings.headline: Chief Financial Officer flags material reservations about budget robustness due to income volatility and unidentified cost pressures
findings.detail: The CFO reports (Section 8.3-8.5) that robust estimates can be given only subject to 'important reservations' including: income from fees and charges in volatile markets and external grants; external competition and declining markets particularly in recession; and cost pressures not identified at budget-setting time including excess inflation. Recommends 'diligent budget monitoring regime' during 2026/27.
findings.matters: The CFO is signalling lack of confidence in the downside risk assessment; this is a warning that actual outcomes could materially exceed budget.
findings.figures: Pay inflation assumption 2026/27: 3.3% (£1,664k); each 1% above assumption costs £290k; non-pay inflation: 2.5% (£172k provision)
findings.quote: Subject to the important reservations below, a reasonable degree of assurance can be given about the robustness of the estimates. The exceptions relate to: (1) The provision of estimates for items outside of the direct control of the Council: Income from fees and charges in volatile markets, and income from grants. External competition and declining markets, particularly during a recession.

findings.headline: Statutory food waste collection service from April 2026 with unclear government funding for ongoing running costs
findings.detail: The Environment Act requires implementation of food waste collections from April 2026. Government provided capital grant for implementation but has not clearly indicated ongoing revenue funding for running costs. The councils assumed the service would be delivered 'to the extent that it was funded' due to financial challenges. The budget now includes £1.48m for this service, but capital requirement for full rollout is still 'to be undertaken'.
findings.matters: A statutory service with uncertain funding creates a contingent liability; if government does not fund the ongoing costs, the councils must absorb them or risk service failure and potential enforcement action.
findings.figures: Food Waste implementation budget 2026/27: £1,480,000; expected ongoing cost per MTFP: £1,530k (2027/28), £1,580k (2028/29)
findings.quote: However, what was not made available was any indication of central new burdens funding allocations for the ongoing running costs of this new service, without this information both councils, due to the financial challenges, assumed that the service would be delivered to the extent that it was funded

findings.headline: Asymmetric financial positions between Adur and Worthing create partnership viability risk
findings.detail: The councils acknowledge that their financial positions are not the same and that asymmetry in capacity creates risk for the shared service arrangement which has operated since 2007. This is described as 'a considerable risk for both councils and the share service arrangement' and requires that capacity differences be addressed in the shared delivery model.
findings.matters: If one partner deteriorates faster than the other, the partnership structure itself could destabilise, forcing unplanned separation and disruption to service continuity.
findings.figures: Adur allocation 2026/27: £13,249k; Worthing allocation 2026/27: £18,240k (58% of total cost)
findings.quote: However, the financial positions of the two councils are not the same. This brings with it risk for the partnership as any asymmetry in the capacity of each council needs to be addressed in the shared delivery model. It remains a considerable risk for both councils and the share service arrangement.

findings.headline: Final government settlement not confirmed; budget built on provisional figures with risk managed through reserves
findings.detail: The budget for 2026/27 is based on a provisional settlement announced 17 December 2025. The final settlement was expected in early February 2026 with a consultation closing 14 January 2026. The council explicitly flags 'a potential risk of a reduction in local funding allocations' and states this risk 'will initially be managed through reserve provisions, but a significant reduction may necessitate decisions affecting the joint service budget'.
findings.matters: If final settlement is lower than provisional, the council has no identified mitigation beyond drawing down reserves, which are already under pressure from structural deficits.
findings.figures: 2026/27 net cost to be funded: £31,489k; management approach: reserve provisions initially, then service budget decisions
findings.quote: The final settlement is expected in early February 2026 with a potential risk of a reduction in local funding allocations. This risk will initially be managed through reserve provisions, but a significant reduction may necessitate decisions affecting the joint service budget.
