findings.headline: Strategic property investment capacity removed due to anticipated regulatory uncertainty from Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards
findings.detail: Adur removed its Strategic Property Investment Fund (invest-to-save provision) after reassessing future Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) regulations that are not yet law but will create significant financial uncertainty for non-compliant commercial properties. Council now focused on maintaining existing portfolio rather than acquisitions.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that forward-looking regulatory change (MEES) is forcing councils to narrow their capital strategy and abandon a revenue-generating investment stream, reducing future capacity to improve financial position.
findings.figures: Specific fund amount not quantified in extract
findings.quote: a reassessment was driven in part by future regulatory changes in the legislation around leasing of commercial premises, specifically, Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) which, though not yet written into law, will introduce significant financial uncertainty for investments that do not comply with the new rules.

findings.headline: Both councils have fixed borrowing caps at maximum sustainable levels with no flexibility for additional schemes
findings.detail: Adur's General Fund new borrowing is capped at £1.0m per year; Worthing at £1.5m per year. The Section 151 Officer explicitly determined the total capital programmes presented represent the maximum level of spending considered affordable. Any new scheme requires removal of schemes of equivalent value.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know both councils have exhausted what they believe is sustainable borrowing headroom. There is no capacity to fund additional investment or absorb financial shocks without cutting existing planned schemes.
findings.figures: Adur General Fund borrowing cap £1.0m per year; Worthing £1.5m per year
findings.quote: The Section 151 Officer has determined that the currently presented programmes represent the maximum level of spending considered affordable. Consequently, any proposal to add a new scheme will require the removal of other schemes of an equivalent value from the programme.

findings.paper_title: 2025.11.12 - JSC - Report item 12 - Revs and Bens MRI contract
findings.headline: Entire procurement strategy contingent on Local Government Reorganization; contract includes early termination option to pivot if LGR does not happen
findings.detail: The 5-year extension is explicitly described as a 'strategic, short-term measure' pending LGR outcome. The rationale for not pursuing full re-procurement is that the new unitary authority will need to review Revenues and Benefits provision anyway. The contract includes 6-month termination notice option to align with LGR partners' requirements.
findings.matters: Business case assumes LGR within contract term; if LGR is delayed or restructured differently than expected, the council may be locked into suboptimal long-term commitment with termination costs.
findings.figures: 5-year term (April 2026 – March 2031); 6-month termination notice required
findings.quote: With Local Government Reform (LGR) in the near horizon the new contract is for a period of 5 years with an option to terminate the contract early with 6 months notice. Whilst we don't yet know who we will be partnered with... the extension is a strategic, short-term measure to allow for a planned future procurement to align with LGR

findings.paper_title: 2025.11.12 - JSC - Report item 12 - Revs and Bens MRI contract
findings.headline: Contract extension will cost £541,205 in year one, creating £11,000 annual budget pressure over the contract term
findings.detail: Year 1 cost: £285,000 one-off license fee (to be capitalised) plus £256,205 annual support/maintenance. Annual financing cost for borrowed capital is approximately £65,000. Ongoing costs have increased by £20,000 (new end-of-year services incorporated), offset by £9,000 saving from Development Fund cancellation, leaving net £11,000 annual pressure. Total 5-year contract value is £1,566,025.
findings.matters: Material capital and revenue budget commitments that must be incorporated into 2026/27 MTFS and forward years; the identified £11k annual pressure is unabsorbed by current savings plans.
findings.figures: £285,000 one-off; £256,205/year ongoing (vs £206,727 current); financing costs circa £65,000/year; £20,000 cost increase, offset by £9,000 saving = £11,000 net pressure; total contract value £1,566,025
findings.quote: the renewal of our term license for the system (minimum 5 years) at a cost of £285,000.00 (excluding VAT)... annual financing costs of the associated borrowing of circa £65,000... The £20,000 increase in annual costs will need to be incorporated into the revenue budget... A £9,000 saving has been identified... leaves a remaining pressure of £11,000

findings.paper_title: 2025.11.12 - JSC - Report item 12 - Revs and Bens MRI contract
findings.headline: Critical system faces expiry in March 2026; council lacks plan B to prevent revenue collection failure
findings.detail: The MRI Revenues and Benefits system is essential for collecting council tax and business rates and administering housing benefit. The current contract expires 31 March 2026. Full re-procurement was considered unviable due to 2-3 year implementation timescales and impending Local Government Reorganization. The council is extending for 5 years to ensure continuity.
findings.matters: Revenue collection failure would immediately impact cash position and statutory service delivery. Delay in procurement decision creates execution risk.
findings.figures: Current contract in place since 1999 (Worthing) and 2005 (Adur); 2-3 years needed for alternative implementation
findings.quote: the implementation and migration to a new system would take a minimum of 2-3 years, and there would be significant disruption and dual-running costs. With the expected Local Government Re-organisation due within this timeframe it was not considered viable

findings.paper_title: 2025.12.09 - JSC - Report item 10 - Refreshing Adur and Worthing Growth Deals with West Sussex County Council
findings.headline: Council is advancing major capital projects during Local Government Reorganisation, creating execution uncertainty.
findings.detail: The paper emphasises multiple times that growth projects are being pushed forward 'even amidst Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and Government Devolution.' LGR is scheduled to happen before some of these projects are completed, which means the merged council structure will inherit these commitments and delivery obligations. This creates uncertainty about governance, staffing, and delivery capacity during a period of significant organizational change.
findings.matters: LGR creates operational and financial risk. Councils undergoing major structural change often struggle with capital project delivery. If projects slip or costs overrun during LGR, the new authority may face financial pressure or service disruption.
findings.figures: Seven projects in Adur portfolio, seven in Worthing, all advancing during LGR period (2025-2030)
findings.quote: Advancing local growth plans and projects is crucial, even amidst Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and Government Devolution. These reforms set out a proposal for greater freedoms and flexibilities at a local level to deliver more effective and better-targeted public services, foster greater growth, and strengthen partnerships between public, private, and community leaders.

findings.paper_title: 2025.12.09 - JSC - Report item 10 - Refreshing Adur and Worthing Growth Deals with West Sussex County Council
findings.headline: Project delivery depends on securing external funding sources that have not yet been confirmed.
findings.detail: The paper states that multiple funding sources beyond the committed pooled business rates will be required to deliver the projects, including CIL/S106 contributions, central government grants, lottery funding, and private sector investment. For example, Southwick FC requires external grant funding and stakeholder match funding in addition to the £500k committed. No timeline or probability of securing these sources is provided.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed external funding creates delivery risk. If additional sources don't materialize, either projects won't be completed as planned or the council will need to fund shortfalls from its own reserves or borrowing.
findings.figures: £500k committed to Southwick FC, with additional external funding sources required but unspecified; £402k committed to Worthing projects with similar dependencies
findings.quote: It is expected that a number of funding sources will be required to deliver the projects within the Deal, including the possibility of capital funding from both parties' capital programmes as well as, collectively, sourcing external funding such as CIL / S106, central government, lottery funding and private sector investment.

findings.paper_title: 2025.12.09 - JSC - Report item 10 - Refreshing Adur and Worthing Growth Deals with West Sussex County Council
findings.headline: Adur committed £500k from Pooled Business Rates to Southwick FC over two years, contingent on business case approval.
findings.detail: The council has been allocated £520k total pooled business rates funding from WSCC, of which £500k is for Southwick FC regeneration (£332k in 2025/26 and £168k in 2026/27) and £20k for Lancing Public Realm. The Southwick FC funding is conditional on approval of a business case at the Member Growth Board. This is a significant capital commitment for a district council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's capital commitments and delivery track record. Large project commitments that require subsequent approvals create execution risk.
findings.figures: £500k for Southwick FC (£332k and £168k across two years), £20k for Lancing Public Realm, from £520k total allocation
findings.quote: An allocation of £520k PBR was issued in February '25 which has been discussed in the Adur Member Growth Board, in specific reference to committing towards Lancing Public Realm detailed design (£20k) and a commitment to Southwick Football Club project (£500k). This paper recommends for ADC, as the project lead, to accept the funding for both projects into ADC accounts over three payments of £20k (Lancing public realm), and for Southwick FC, £332k in 25/26 and a further £168k in 26/27.

findings.headline: Both councils are planning to rebuild reserves but Worthing cannot make any contribution this year, leaving Adur to rebuild alone while carrying statutory pressures
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget set out plans to rebuild reserve balances. For Adur, budgeted contributions were £950k to Property Risk Reserve and £300k for general reserves. For Worthing, £750k and £1,036k respectively. However, the paper states 'Worthing council will not be in a position to meet the budgeted contribution to reserves'. Adur is projected to contribute £993k (mostly to Property Investment Risk Reserve), but even this assumes the underspend holds. If either council faces a deterioration, reserve rebuilding will be further delayed, leaving them more vulnerable.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is occurring across both councils. Only Adur has headroom to rebuild, and even that is contingent on maintaining current performance. Worthing is in a downward spiral: cannot rebuild reserves, statutory pressures grow, reserves will continue to fall.
findings.figures: Adur: budgeted contributions £1,250k (£950k Property Risk + £300k general); actual forecast £993k; Worthing: budgeted contributions £1,786k (£750k Property Risk + £1,036k general); actual: £0
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget set out plans to begin rebuilding reserve balance for both councils, however any transfer is limited to the outturn position and current indications are that Worthing council will not be in a position to meet the budgeted contribution to reserves.

findings.headline: Adur Housing Revenue Account is forecasting an £858k overspend driven by void properties (£727k) which require carrying costs after tenant exit
findings.detail: The Adur HRA budget assumed 97 properties vacant (3.8% void rate). However, the actual forecast shows 'Rent & Service Charge loss due to void properties' of £727k, plus additional council tax liabilities and lost service charges. The paper also forecasts repairs and maintenance overspend of £104k. This means void property management is a material cost pressure. The forecast requires a withdrawal of £701,704 from the General Reserve (which will fall from £1,219,884 to £518,180).
findings.matters: Void properties in the HRA are a deadweight cost (no rent income, full liability for rates, maintenance, and service charges). High voids suggest either poor lettability, rapid turnover, or holding stock off-market. This drains reserves and signals potential housing stock quality issues.
findings.figures: HRA overspend £858k; void property loss £727k; repairs & maintenance overspend £104k; General Reserve withdrawal £701,704; vacancy budget 3.8% (97 properties)
findings.quote: The most significant pressures are due to: Void properties (including losses in associated service charges and increased Council Tax liabilities) - £727k. Repairs and maintenance - £104k.

findings.headline: Worthing Integrated Care Centre has not opened as planned, costing £346k in lost rental income, and another strategic property was sold, creating a further £379k shortfall
findings.detail: The paper forecasts a £278k net surplus in strategic property for Worthing, but this assumes 'the budgeted transfer of the void allowance to the Property Investment Risk Reserve will not be made'. The underlying position is worse: the Worthing Integrated Care Centre 'not being opened' creates a 'rental shortfall of £346K', and 'one of the assets has now been sold, thus creating an income rental shortfall of £379K'. Additional void losses from two smaller assets add to the pressure. The paper indicates capital scheme timelines are slipping.
findings.matters: Planned capital projects and asset disposals are slipping, which affects both cash flow (delayed disposals reduce near-term cash) and borrowing forecasts. This indicates project delivery risk.
findings.figures: WICC opening delay: £346k rental shortfall; asset sale: £379k lost rental income; net strategic property position assumes void allowance transfer not made
findings.quote: The Worthing Integrated Community Centre not being opened, with a rental shortfall of £346K expected. Additionally, one of the assets has now been sold, thus creating an income rental shortfall of £379K.

findings.headline: Bereavement services (crematorium and cemetery) face structural decline: death rates are lower than budget and funeral directors are opening competing chapels, creating £625k loss in Worthing and £57k in Adur
findings.detail: The paper attributes the shortfall to 'a lower-than-anticipated death rate, reflecting a downturn seen across the national sector'. Additionally, 'income continues to be affected by local competition, as other crematoria offer discounted rates to large funeral directors, and many funeral directors are continuing to invest in developing their own chapels'. Bookings are 'shifting towards unattended direct cremations' which generate lower margins, while 'bookings for higher-margin attended cremations have fallen'. A commercial review was completed and recommendations are being phased in (memorial garden opened, memorial plot sales commenced), but the underlying market challenge remains.
findings.matters: Bereavement services are a discretionary revenue source. The council faces both demand headwinds (lower death rates, demographic/health factors) and competitive pressure (funeral industry consolidating). The income is likely to remain under pressure.
findings.figures: Worthing bereavement services deficit £625k (crematorium £686k shortfall partially offset by cemetery and memorials); Adur deficit £57k
findings.quote: The bereavement service continues to deliver a net surplus, but faces a £625k deficit against its budget target in Worthing. Despite a budget reset for 24/25 that reduced income targets by £500k following a commercial review, a shortfall persists. This variance is also attributable to a lower-than-anticipated death rate, reflecting a downturn seen across the national sector.

findings.headline: Planning application income has collapsed: major applications have fallen from ~2 per month to single figures per annum, creating £369k shortfall in Worthing and £98k in Adur
findings.detail: Planning income is 'largely demand led and can therefore fluctuate making forecasting difficult to predict'. Historically there were 'an average of around 2 major applications each month across Adur & Worthing', but 'in the years since the pandemic this has slipped to single figures per annum'. A single major application generates between £20k and £30k in fees (compared to just over £500 for a householder application). The paper notes that 'the government's National Planning Policy Framework consultation of 2024 acknowledged that local planning authorities particularly those who receive few large major applications, are vulnerable to large funding shortfalls' which 'remains the case at the Councils'. There are some signs of pickup (4 major applications received since June), but recovery is uncertain.
findings.matters: Planning fee income is highly concentrated in a small number of transactions. The council cannot control whether major developments are proposed. This creates both volatility and downside risk if the local economy weakens.
findings.figures: Worthing shortfall £369k; Adur shortfall £98k; historical rate ~2 major applications per month; current rate single figures per annum; single major application fee £20k-£30k vs householder £500+
findings.quote: In the years since the pandemic this has slipped to single figures per annum... the government's National Planning Policy Framework consultation of 2024 acknowledged that local planning authorities particularly those who receive few large major applications, are vulnerable to large funding shortfalls which remains the case at the Councils.

findings.headline: Worthing car parks are forecasting a £685k income shortfall driven by structural change (increased remote working) and the closure of Grafton Car Park
findings.detail: Parking income is 'impacted by long-term structural changes, such as increased remote working' that have moved 'beyond a short-term pandemic effect to become a new normal'. Grafton Car Park closed on 16 May, costing £677k against budget. The paper notes this closure 'has not caused any immediate capacity pressures' because 'Worthing has generally had excess capacity', but there has been 'displacement to other council owned car parks' and private alternatives. The paper forecasts a total shortfall of £685k, of which £468k is income shortfall.
findings.matters: A major revenue stream is being permanently eroded by changes outside the council's control. This is not cyclical; it reflects a structural shift in working patterns that will not reverse. The asset (car parks) is stranded capacity.
findings.figures: Total car park shortfall £685k; income shortfall £468k; Grafton Car Park closure impact £677k
findings.quote: Worthing car park income continues to be one of the main income streams that is most impacted by long-term structural changes, such as increased remote working. This shift in working patterns has altered demand for parking, moving beyond a short-term pandemic effect to become a new normal.

findings.headline: Worthing's central government homelessness prevention grant is disproportionately low despite having the second-highest number of households in temporary accommodation in the county
findings.detail: The paper reveals a mismatch between need and funding. Worthing received £1,175 per homeless household in 2024/25, compared to the West Sussex average of £4,917 — a shortfall of £3,742 per claim. Adur received £2,464 vs the average £4,917, a shortfall of £2,453. The paper states this is 'understood to be a legacy allocation relating to incorrect data going back over 5 years' and despite Worthing having 'the second highest number of households in temporary accommodation in the county as at the end of the 2024/25 financial year', funding remains 'disproportionate'. Senior officers have 'been in discussion with MHCLG regarding financial pressures' but 'resolution is expected to take time'.
findings.matters: Central government funding is not matching actual need or service delivery. A lender should know the councils are lobbying for fairer allocation but remain underfunded in a critical area, with no guarantee of change.
findings.figures: Worthing HPG per household 2024/25: £1,175 (vs West Sussex average £4,917); Worthing variation to average: -£3,742; Adur: £2,464 (vs average £4,917, variation -£2,453)
findings.quote: Worthing has the second highest number of households in temporary accommodation in the county as at the end of the 2024/25 financial year... this legacy allocation relates to incorrect data going back over 5 years and we are still impacted

findings.headline: Homelessness caseloads are driving an £881k overspend in Adur and £3,032k in Worthing, with statutory duties preventing cost control
findings.detail: Homelessness is the single largest pressure across both councils. New approaches in Q2 reached 119 in Adur (up from 96 last year) and 335 in Worthing (up from 329). The paper states the councils 'are moving increasingly away from reduced government funding' but homelessness is a statutory duty where 'many of the council's responsibilities in this area are statutory, limiting their ability to control spending'. The Housing Needs transformation team is working to shift cases from crisis (relief) stage to prevention earlier, and efforts include building owned temporary accommodation. However, 'the existing number of households in temporary accommodation will continue to be a cost pressure due to lack of move on options'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the councils cannot simply cut homelessness spending. These are statutory duties where demand is driven by external factors (housing shortage, rental costs) outside their control, creating unpredictable and rising costs.
findings.figures: Adur homelessness overspend £881k; Worthing homelessness overspend £3,032k; new approaches Q2: Adur 119 (vs 96 prior year), Worthing 335 (vs 329 prior year)
findings.quote: Cost pressures continue to persist in discharging our statutory duties due to the steady number of cases involving individuals, couples, and families presenting to the council homeless... many of the council's responsibilities in this area are statutory, limiting their ability to control spending.

findings.headline: Worthing's reserves will be exhausted by the projected overspend and remain £534,538 short
findings.detail: Worthing holds £1,580,929 in available reserves but is forecasting a £2,115,467 overspend for 2025/26. After using all reserves to cover the shortfall, there would be a deficit of £534,538. The council's policy is to maintain reserves at 6-10% of net revenue expenditure; the current balance represents only 4.2% and will be entirely depleted. The council has applied to MHCLG for exceptional funding support, but officers note that 'resolution is expected to take time' and councils 'must, at least in the near term, absorb the financial pressure'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot weather unexpected shocks and depends on government bail-out funding which may not materialise. This is a fundamental solvency question.
findings.figures: Overspend £2,115,467; available reserves £1,580,929; resulting shortfall £534,538; General Fund Working Balance £755,482 (4.2% of net revenue expenditure against a policy range of 6-10%)
findings.quote: Worthing Borough Council holds a limited level of available reserves (excluding the Tax Smoothing Reserve and Grants and Contributions). The utilisation of these reserves remains a matter for concern as it will impact the council's ability to absorb financial shocks in future years

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 allocation will not be visible until mid-December, creating planning uncertainty
findings.detail: The new funding formula methodology, which is supposed to direct funding to areas of high demand (including temporary accommodation), will not be announced until 'the week commencing 15th December'. The paper states 'there is a significant level of uncertainty on the local impact of the new assessment formula'. Assumptions in the current MTFP are based on external advisor modelling, not actual allocations.
findings.matters: Budget planning without knowing actual funding creates cash-flow and delivery risk. If allocations are lower than assumed, deficits widen immediately. If higher, the council may have to revise but cannot rely on it.
findings.figures: Settlement expected week of 15 December; current assumptions based on Pixel Financial Management Ltd modelling of government proposals
findings.quote: there is a significant level of uncertainty on the local impact of the new assessment formula. The allocation across individual councils will not be visible until the provisional settlement which is not expected until the week commencing 15th December

findings.headline: Capital borrowing is increasing and carrying higher financing costs
findings.detail: The councils are planning additional prudential borrowing of £1.5m for Worthing and £1m for Adur in 2026/27. Financing costs on the capital programme are rising by £293k for Worthing and £213k for Adur. The paper also notes councils will 'experience the impact of historical borrowing for some time as debts which were taken on at low rates of interest need to be refinanced as the loan periods mature'.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs squeeze revenue budgets further. Refinancing of historical debt at higher rates creates a structural headwind. This compounds the revenue deficits and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Worthing £1.5m additional borrowing; Adur £1m; financing costs up £293k and £213k respectively in 2026/27; average borrowing rate assumed at 4.60% in 2026/27, falling to 4.00% by 2028/29
findings.quote: the level of additional borrowing is set at £1.5m for Worthing and £1m for Adur... This financial assumption together with the impact of the current programme and refinancing requirements has increased the financing costs revenue budget requirement in 2026/27 by £293k in Worthing and £213k in Adur

findings.headline: Supported accommodation costs are growing exponentially due to gap between housing benefit rates (set in 2011) and actual placement costs
findings.detail: Adur and Worthing have 'disproportionately high allocation of supported accommodation placements' that have 'increased exponentially over the last 3 years'. The gap exists because housing benefit is 'linked to the 2011 Local Housing Allowance', while placement costs have risen. The councils must meet the cost of the differential. Officers have been communicating with MHCLG and DWP but this remains a structural problem.
findings.matters: A funding gap built into national benefit policy and widening year-on-year is effectively a subsidy from local budgets to national policy. It is neither controllable nor fixable at council level. Adur received £225k additional allocation in 2025/26, Worthing £1m, but the problem is not solved.
findings.figures: £1m increase for Worthing in 2025/26; £225k for Adur in 2025/26; placements 'increased exponentially over the last 3 years'
findings.quote: Councils have to meet the cost of the differential between the benefits paid out for accommodation, and the subsidy that can be reclaimed which is linked to the 2011 Local Housing Allowance

findings.headline: Government food waste funding will be hidden in the settlement formula with councils likely to be underfunded
findings.detail: The government has confirmed it will provide 'new burdens funding for the ongoing revenue cost of operating weekly food waste collections'. However, this funding will be 'rolled into the finance settlement and distributed via the main funding formula rather than via a specific grant'. The paper states this means 'there will be no transparency about how much new burdens funding is provided and a likelihood that some, if not all, councils will be underfunded for the costs'.
findings.matters: A mandated service with opaque, likely-insufficient funding creates an unquantifiable future liability. The council cannot know whether funding will cover costs or whether the gap will widen over time. The joint services budget shows £1,450k annual cost.
findings.figures: £1,450k annual cost to joint services in 2026/27
findings.quote: there will be no transparency about how much new burdens funding is provided and a likelihood that some, if not all, councils will be underfunded for the costs of introducing a full food waste collection service

findings.headline: Budget deficits are forecast to grow throughout the planning period, from £2.76m to £5.65m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The joint cumulative shortfall grows from £2,760k in 2026/27 to £5,648k in 2030/31. For Worthing specifically, it rises from £3,787k to £5,785k. Even Adur, which shows a small surplus in 2026/27, faces growing deficits from 2027/28 onwards (£432k to £1,222k by 2030/31). The paper does not identify where these recurring deficits will be closed.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit implies either repeated exceptional support, progressive service cuts, or asset sales. None are sustainable. A lender sees a council whose core revenues are not keeping pace with its costs, with no end in sight.
findings.figures: 2026/27: Joint £2,760k, Worthing £3,787k, Adur (£27k); 2030/31: Joint £5,648k, Worthing £5,785k, Adur £1,222k
findings.quote: Despite the considerable work being done to implement a more resilient and sustainable financial strategy, it is clear that... the projected cumulative shortfall [grows from] 2,760 [to] 5,648

findings.headline: Worthing is spending 31% of its net revenue budget on temporary and emergency accommodation
findings.detail: Housing demand, including temporary accommodation and supported accommodation placements, has grown exponentially and now dominates the budget. The paper notes this is 'despite ongoing investment on prevention work' and explicitly states the council is 'having to run to stay still' on this pressure. An additional £1m has been built into the 2026/27 budget specifically for housing, on top of the £1m increase already approved for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A single demand-driven line consuming nearly a third of revenue budget is a critical vulnerability. It is driven by external factors (housing benefit rates, commissioning by other bodies) outside the council's control and shows no sign of stabilizing. This crowds out other services and leaves no reserves for emergencies.
findings.figures: 31% of Worthing net revenue budget; Adur 16%; £1m additional allocation for housing in 2026/27 plus £1m in 2025/26; supported accommodation placements 'increased exponentially over the last 3 years'
findings.quote: forecasting to spend circa 31% of the Worthing and 16% of the Adur net revenue budgets on this alone

findings.headline: Worthing requires exceptional financial support to balance a £3.787m budget gap in 2026/27
findings.detail: The financial strategy is insufficient to close Worthing's projected shortfall. The paper recommends the chief executive formally request Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from MHCLG. This is not new — Worthing received EFS for 2025/26 using capital flexibility — but the paper expects continued support 'for the foreseeable future unless there are significant changes in government funding for homelessness'.
findings.matters: A council dependent on exceptional government support signals financial instability and inability to manage within its funding envelope. Lenders assess governance risk and sustainability; reliance on ad-hoc central funding suggests structural imbalance.
findings.figures: Worthing £3,787k shortfall in 2026/27; cumulative shortfall growing to £5,785k by 2030/31
findings.quote: it is clear that it is unlikely to provide the funding required to close the significant budget gap in Worthing and so the proposed route for requesting exceptional funding support (EFS) which is outlined in the policy statement is necessary

findings.paper_title: Joint 2nd Capital Investment Programme & Projects Monitoring 2025-26
findings.headline: Nearly one third of Adur capital schemes now flagged as requiring close monitoring, indicating elevated programme risk
findings.detail: Revised scheme categorisation at Q1 now highlights projects with resourcing, timeliness or interdependency risks. findings.matters: When nearly a third of a council's capital schemes require close monitoring, it signals elevated delivery risk and the need for active council oversight and management of capital performance.
findings.figures: Adur: 22 of 71 (30.99%) closely monitored, 3 (4.23%) with significant challenges; Worthing: 15 of 71 (21.13%) closely monitored, 1 (1.41%) with challenges
findings.quote: This new approach has significantly increased the population of the section 'Schemes where progress is being closely monitored' for both councils.

findings.detail: Capital scheme expenditure has been delayed due to vacancies across the housing projects team and HRA surveying team, which limited progress in late 2024 and early 2025. These resource gaps, combined with challenges from prior year schemes, continue to constrain capacity for new scheme delivery.

findings.detail: The Sussex Yacht Club flood defence scheme has faced multiple challenges since inception. The council is pursuing additional funding through the Environment Agency, with a final report to JSC expected 9 December.

Work on site is delayed while officers verify the council's contractual rights and any performance bond claims.
findings.matters: Contractor failure on housing schemes is a material delivery and financial risk that may result in cost increases, extended delays, or loss of investment designed to house residents in need.

findings.paper_title: 2025.11.12 - JSC - Agenda Item 7 - Review of the Council Tax Support Schemes in Adur and Worthing
findings.headline: CTS caseload and costs difficult to forecast amid economic uncertainty
findings.detail: Worthing's costs jumped 15.62% when it removed a £5 weekly charge in 2023/24 (from £5,679k to £6,566k). Both councils acknowledge forecasting the demand-led scheme is unreliable because it responds to economic conditions and cost-of-living impacts, which remain volatile.
findings.matters: Unpredictable demand-led budget pressures in a scheme the councils cannot easily adjust (given political commitments to vulnerable residents) create a budget risk that could force choices elsewhere if economic conditions worsen.
findings.figures: Worthing CTS jumped from £5,679k (2022/23) to £6,566k (2023/24, +15.62%) following removal of £5 weekly restriction; rose again to £6,896k (2024/25, +5.02%) and estimated £7,155k (2025/26).
findings.quote: It remains difficult to forecast caseload and expenditure with any degree of certainty in the backdrop of the current economic climate and the enduring impacts of the cost of living on many of our communities.

findings.paper_title: 2025.11.12 - JSC - Agenda Item 7 - Review of the Council Tax Support Schemes in Adur and Worthing
findings.headline: Council tax collection rates declining during cost-of-living crisis
findings.detail: In-year collection rates have declined at both councils in recent years. Adur fell from 97.07% in 2021/22 to 96.44% in 2024/25. The paper explicitly attributes this to cost-of-living pressures and redesign of the revenues team during digital transformation.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates mean actual council tax income lags budget during a period when the councils are already facing extreme budget pressures and CTS costs are rising unpredictably.
findings.figures: Adur: 96.44% (2024/25), down 0.63pp from 2021/22 peak. Worthing: 96.53% (2024/25), down 0.41pp from 2023/24. Both councils report collection below prior-year rates.
findings.quote: Council Tax collection has remained challenging due to the continued 'cost of living' situation. With the current budget pressures and redesign of the Revenues team, whilst we undergo digital transformation programme for the service, collection rates remain comparably with neighbouring authorities.

findings.paper_title: 2025.11.12 - JSC - Agenda Item 7 - Review of the Council Tax Support Schemes in Adur and Worthing
findings.headline: Growing unfunded gap in Council Tax Support costs as government funding shrinks
findings.detail: The councils must now fund locally an increasing share of CTS costs because the government grant was consolidated into Revenue Support Grant, which has since ceased entirely. Adur must fund £279.5k locally (38.6% shortfall) and Worthing £349.2k (41.5% shortfall) in 2025/26. This is an ever-growing budget pressure with no clear resolution.
findings.matters: A persistent and growing unfunded budget pressure reduces financial flexibility and crowds out other spending during a period both councils acknowledge as involving extreme budgetary pressure.
findings.figures: Adur 2025/26: net cost £279.5k with 38.6% shortfall in funding (government covers only 61.4%). Worthing 2025/26: net cost £349.2k with 41.5% shortfall (government covers only 58.5%).
findings.quote: the grant towards the cost of Council Tax Support Schemes has been consolidated into the Revenue Support Grant and the retained Business Rates scheme. The combined income from these sources has fallen each year, and the Revenue Support Grant has now ceased as a source of income to the councils. This means that the councils have faced an ever-increasing cost associated with the scheme.

findings.headline: The Fairer Funding Review outcome poses a significant risk to the council's financial stability and ability to deliver its strategy
findings.detail: The Sustainability & Risk Assessment section identifies national economic uncertainty and the government's Fairer Funding Review as a material risk to financial stability. The timing of this review outcome is critical to the council's ability to fully implement its three-year corporate strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty on the council's funding base; an adverse Fairer Funding Review outcome could materially constrain the council's financial position and ability to maintain services.

findings.headline: Worthing's investment income falling as interest rates decline and asset disposal proceeds underperform
findings.detail: Worthing is projecting investment income to decline from £172k in 2026/27 to negative £217k (a cost) by 2030/31, as interest rates fall toward the 2% Bank of England target and capital receipts from planned asset disposals do not materialize at expected levels.
findings.matters: Councils that budget for investment income are vulnerable if asset sales fail to happen or interest rates fall faster; this reduces financial headroom and typically forces further savings
findings.figures: Worthing investment interest projected at £172k (2026/27) falling to negative £217k (2030/31)
findings.quote: In Worthing this has been compounded by a reduction in the forecast income from investment, impacted by both a fall in interest rates and the assumed level of capital receipts from the asset disposal programme.

findings.headline: Government funding reform is unresolved; final settlement not due until late December, after budget must be formally set
findings.detail: The government is consulting on a Fair Funding Review that will restructure local government funding from 2026/27 onwards. Final policy positions will not be announced until autumn, and draft determinations will not be issued until late December. The MTFP is based on external consultants' modelling of proposals, not confirmed amounts.
findings.matters: Budget projections built on uncertain government policy create cliff risks; if actual funding is lower than assumed, councils face emergency spending cuts or further support applications
findings.figures: Assumptions based on Pixel Financial Management modelling of government consultation, not confirmed allocations
findings.quote: The final funding allocation is therefore not yet known and draft determinations will not be notified to local authorities until the Provisional Settlement which is due late December.

findings.detail: The MTFP includes revenue impacts from these long-term commitments totalling £846k in 2026/27. Individual project impacts are not separately disclosed, but line shows ongoing obligation.
findings.matters: Major capital projects often generate hidden ongoing revenue costs; if any underperforms (lower sale proceeds, higher operating costs, delays), it will worsen the budget deficit

findings.quote: the Worthing Integrated Care Centre, the closure of the Grafton MSCP and the sale of Union Place for development.

findings.headline: Worthing's capital financing costs rising sharply, with interest on borrowing growing from £282k to £680k over 5 years
findings.detail: Interest on capital borrowing is projected to more than double as Worthing takes on £1.5m of new prudential borrowing and refinances maturing debt at higher rates. This has already forced a £260k increase to the 2026/27 revenue budget just to cover higher financing costs.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs indicate growing debt service burden that will crowd out service spending; if interest rates stay elevated or rise further, available resources will shrink
findings.figures: Worthing interest on borrowing: £282k (2026/27) to £680k (2030/31); revenue budget impact up £260k in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: financing costs revenue budget requirement in 2026/27 by £260k in Worthing and £180k in Adur.

findings.headline: Budget shortfalls are solved by 'assumed' savings from organisational restructuring that have not yet been identified
findings.detail: The MTFP is built on the assumption that organisational design work will deliver its financial targets, but the document explicitly states these savings are merely 'assumed' without specifying what they are. This is work in progress.
findings.matters: A budget built on unidentified savings is not credible; lenders need to know whether the council has a realistic plan or is gambling on internal restructuring delivering the required amounts

findings.headline: Worthing's Housing Needs service continues to overspend even after budget increases
findings.detail: The council has already invested Housing Prevention Grant funding into the Housing Needs service in 2025/26, yet projections indicate it will continue to overspend. The budget includes a service increase from 2026/27 but even this is expected to be insufficient.
findings.matters: A service that overspends despite additional funding signals demand is outpacing any realistic budget allocation; this creates risk of uncontrolled overspends in future years

findings.quote: The council has approved some in-year investment of the Housing Prevention Grant into the Housing Needs service however current projections indicate a continuing overspend in the service.

findings.headline: Worthing faces a £4.1m budget deficit in 2026/27 requiring continued Exceptional Funding Support from government
findings.detail: Worthing's budget shortfall is £4,095k in 2026/27, growing to £5,830k by 2030/31. The council has already required government Exceptional Funding Support (capital flexibility) to balance 2025/26 and expects to continue requiring EFS for the foreseeable future.
findings.matters: A council that cannot balance without government emergency funding signals financial distress; lenders assess credit risk partly on whether a council must seek government support, and the trigger for more intensive oversight
findings.figures: Worthing 2026/27 shortfall £4,095k; 2030/31 £5,830k
findings.quote: It is expected that Worthing will continue to require support through the EFS scheme for the foreseeable future unless there are significant changes in funding for homelessness.

findings.paper_title: Joint 1st Capital Investment Programme & Projects Monitoring 2025-26
findings.headline: Worthing's Grafton car park has closed after unexpected concrete failure, raising serious doubts about the effectiveness of the council's annual structural maintenance programme.
findings.detail: A section of concrete failed without visible warning signs. The failure has prompted structural engineers to re-evaluate the ongoing repair program after years of planned annual structural works, suggesting the maintenance strategy has not been effective.
findings.matters: A council asset has failed unexpectedly after a years-long maintenance programme, indicating either poor asset condition assessment or ineffective maintenance execution, with implications for other council assets.

findings.paper_title: Joint 1st Capital Investment Programme & Projects Monitoring 2025-26
findings.headline: Contractor collapse has left Adur's Albion Street housing scheme stalled with a £465k cost overrun.
findings.detail: The design and build contractor Westridge Construction has gone into administration, leaving the scheme unable to proceed. An overspend of £465,456 from 2024/25 must be covered by virement from the Adur Homes carry-forward budget. A separate report on the project's position is pending and will address the service charge position.
findings.matters: A major capital housing scheme is stuck with no clear path forward, and the council has already absorbed nearly half a million in cost overruns.
findings.figures: £465,456 overspend on Albion Street; £18m commitment for Adur Homes schemes in 2025/26
findings.quote: The project to deliver new properties for Adur Homes at the Albion Street Site continues to face challenges following the collapse of the design and build contractor Westridge Construction into administration.

findings.headline: Adur's Housing Revenue Account (HRA) is forecast to overspend by £713k, driven by void properties and repair costs.
findings.detail: Adur's HRA (the ring-fenced account for council housing) is forecast to overspend £713k. The main pressures are void properties (empty rental units incurring losses and council tax liabilities): £598k, and repairs & maintenance overspend: £104k. This is partially offset by a £57k underspend in employee costs due to vacancies. The void position indicates either asset management issues or structural challenges in lettings.
findings.matters: HRA overspend can trigger the need for central government approval of borrowing or may require general fund subsidies, constraining the council's overall financial flexibility.
findings.figures: HRA overspend forecast: £713k. Void property losses: £598k. Repairs & maintenance overspend: £104k. Staff underspend: (£57k).
findings.quote: The HRA is forecast to overspend against the budget for 2025/26 by £713k. The most significant pressures are due to: Void properties (including losses in associated service charges and increased Council Tax liabilities) - £598k. Repairs and maintenance - £104k.

findings.headline: The £2.365m organisational design programme savings plan is at risk from uncontrollable statutory cost pressures.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget committed to £2.365m in savings from an organisational design programme intended to reposition the council financially for resilience. However, the paper warns: "The continued and growing challenges outlined in this report underscore the importance of the programme's long-term goals... It is also of note that many of these same challenges are associated with statutory duties and risk eroding the progress of spend controls and the design programme in addressing the financial challenge faced by the councils." In plain terms: statutory pressures (homelessness, supported accommodation) are eating into savings delivered by the restructure, putting the financial strategy at risk.
findings.matters: If the savings plan is failing to deliver net benefit because statutory pressures are growing faster than the programme can save, the council's financial strategy is broken and will not achieve planned sustainability.
findings.figures: Organisational design programme savings target: £2.365m. Homelessness overspend (Worthing): £2.267m; (Adur) £598k. Supported accommodation cost (Worthing): £800k.
findings.quote: Many of these same challenges are associated with statutory duties and risk eroding the progress of spend controls and the design programme in addressing the financial challenge faced by the councils.

findings.headline: Worthing required £2m in exceptional government funding support to balance the budget and applied for it due to financial distress.
findings.detail: The forecast outturn shows Worthing with a £4.034m operational overspend before government support. The council applied to MHCLG for financial support through the Exceptional Funding Support scheme for 2025/26 and received £2m, bringing the overspend down to £2.034m (of which £1.469m remains after reserves transfers). The paper notes: "Worthing Borough Council holds a limited level of available reserves (excluding the Tax Smoothing Reserve and Grants and Contributions). The utilisation of these reserves remains a matter for concern as it will impact the council's ability to absorb financial shocks in future years and this is a key driver for continued efforts to improve the Council's financial standing."
findings.matters: Requiring central government emergency funding signals acute financial distress and is a red flag for creditworthiness. It indicates the council cannot balance its budget through its own resources and savings efforts.
findings.figures: Exceptional Funding Support received: £2,000k. Overspend before support: £4,034k. Overspend after support: £2,034k.
findings.quote: In recognition of this position, the Council applied to MHCLG for financial support through the Exceptional Funding Support scheme for the 2025/26 budget year.

findings.headline: Multiple income-dependent service budgets are significantly under-achieving: cremations, burials, planning and building control fees are all down due to weak economic conditions.
findings.detail: Bereavement services (cremations and burials) are forecast £327k down in Worthing and £63k in Adur due to falling cremation volumes and reduced burial income. Planning and development income (building control, development management, land charges) is forecast down £437k in Worthing and £130k in Adur. The paper attributes this to: weak economic conditions, high inflation, high mortgage rates, reduced construction activity, and lack of major planning applications. These are demand-led income streams that the council cannot control.
findings.matters: These income shortfalls reduce the council's flexible revenue and indicate underlying economic weakness in the local economy affecting both council income and residents' financial capacity.
findings.figures: Bereavement: Worthing £327k shortfall, Adur £63k. Planning/Development: Worthing £437k shortfall, Adur £130k. Worthing crematorium alone: £429k income shortfall before expenditure offsets.
findings.quote: The current economic conditions with high inflation and mortgage rates together with high construction costs is having a significant impact on the housing market and development industry. This has had an impact on planning, building control and land charges fee income.

findings.headline: Income from car parking has fallen structurally and will not recover: Worthing is down £404k in Q1 due to permanent shifts to remote working and permanent car park closures.
findings.detail: Worthing car park income is forecast to underachieve by £404k. The biggest hit is Grafton car park closure (16 May), which left a £659k shortfall to budget, partially offset by displacement to other car parks. However, the paper identifies a longer-term structural decline: "Worthing car park income continues to be one of the main income streams that is most impacted by long-term structural changes, such as increased remote working. This shift in working patterns has altered demand for parking, moving beyond a short-term pandemic effect to become a new normal." This is not a temporary pressure but a permanent revenue loss.
findings.matters: Permanent reductions to income streams reduce the council's sustainable revenue base and require permanent spending cuts or other permanent revenue sources to offset.
findings.figures: Worthing car park underspend: £404k (of which £423k income shortfall). Grafton closure impact: £659k shortfall. Adur car parks: £24k underspend (on target due to price increase).
findings.quote: Worthing car park income continues to be one of the main income streams that is most impacted by long-term structural changes, such as increased remote working. This shift in working patterns has altered demand for parking, moving beyond a short-term pandemic effect to become a new normal.

findings.headline: Homelessness caseloads are rising again after a brief plateau, creating uncontrollable statutory cost pressures.
findings.detail: Homelessness is the single largest cost driver in the overspend: £2.267m for Worthing, £598k for Adur. The paper notes the past 3 months have seen "a significant increase in case load" after brief stability. The council has a statutory duty to house homeless individuals and cannot control this spending, even as caseload grows. Central government's homelessness prevention grant (HPG) is disproportionately low: Worthing receives £1,175 per household vs. a regional average of £4,917—a shortfall of £3,742 per household.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory, demand-led cost that the council cannot manage down. With under-funding from central government and rising presentations, this is a structural deficit that will continue to erode financial performance.
findings.figures: Worthing homelessness overspend: £2,267k. Adur: £598k. Worthing HPG funding: £1,175 per household; regional average £4,917. Worthing variation to average: -£3,742. Q1 2025/26 shows temporary caseload stabilisation, but paper assumes reduction in H2 from prevention activities not yet proven.
findings.quote: After statistics briefly suggested that the councils may be reaching a plateau in housing pressures, the past 3 months have seen a significant increase in case load. The increased demand for housing services presents a significant risk to future council finances, primarily because many of the council's responsibilities in this area are statutory, limiting their ability to control spending.

findings.headline: Worthing is dramatically over-exposed to unregistered supported accommodation, creating an £800k annual subsidy gap the council cannot control.
findings.detail: Non-registered supported accommodation units in Worthing have grown 221% since 2021 (from 7 to 159 units). Councils can only claim housing benefit subsidy up to 2011 market rent levels for these properties, meaning the authority must cover the gap between actual rents and the subsidy limit. For 2025/26, this shortfall is forecast at £800k for Worthing, with Adur at £128k. This is being driven by an unregulated market and lack of regulatory powers for councils to restrict supply.
findings.matters: This creates a structural, ongoing cost that will persist and potentially grow, beyond the council's control and outside normal budgeting, directly eroding the council's financial standing.
findings.figures: Worthing: 2171% increase in units (7 in 2021 → 159 in 2025); £800k full-year subsidy shortfall. Adur: £128k full-year shortfall. Q1 actual (01/04/25–31/07/25): Worthing £292,526, Adur £44,436.
findings.quote: If we look at the 2021 figures, we had 7 claims for payment for non registered supported claims in Worthing, in 2025 we have 159, representing a 2171% increase.

findings.headline: Worthing's reserves will fall to critically low levels after funding the forecast overspend.
findings.detail: Worthing's total available reserves of £1.58m will be reduced to £111k after accounting for the forecasted £1.47m overspend. The council's policy is to maintain reserves at 6-10% of net revenue expenditure; this leaves it well below that threshold and severely limits the council's ability to manage unexpected financial pressures.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves mean the council has no buffer for future shocks and undermines financial stability for lenders assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Starting reserves £1,580,929 → Remaining £111,240 after overspend funding. Policy range 6-10% of £17.8m budget = £1.07m–1.78m minimum.
findings.quote: After accounting for the forecasted overspend, the total reserves figure is reduced to £111,240. A draw of reserves of this quantum takes the forecasted reserves position critically below the recommended policy range.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2024-25 ADC and WBC - WIP
findings.headline: Mandatory member training on treasury management was not delivered during 2024-25.
findings.detail: The Prudential Code requires member training on treasury management matters, but the council did not arrange training during 2024-25. Training was eventually delivered on 12 June 2025, after the financial year ended. Members are responsible for scrutiny of treasury activities, so a gap in training during the year represents a governance weakness.
findings.matters: Without trained members providing oversight, the council's treasury and borrowing decisions during 2024-25 lacked the required level of governance scrutiny.
findings.figures: Training delivered 12 June 2025, after year end; requirement under Prudential Code
findings.quote: Member training on treasury management matters is now a requirement of the Prudential Code. Officers were unfortunately unable to arrange training during 2024/25. Since the year end however, a session has been delivered to members by an external trainer on 12th June 2025.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2024-25 ADC and WBC - WIP
findings.headline: Worthing's under-borrowed position fell 80% from £9.068m to £1.827m, leaving minimal cash buffer.
findings.detail: Worthing's under-borrowing — using cash reserves instead of external debt to fund capital needs — fell from £9.068m to £1.827m in one year. As this buffer shrinks, the council loses financial flexibility and must rely more on external borrowing markets if additional capital spending is needed.
findings.matters: Low under-borrowing reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or changes in capital plans without accessing debt markets at potentially unfavourable rates.
findings.figures: Under-borrowed £1.827m at 31 March 2025, down from £9.068m at 31 March 2024
findings.quote: Worthing Borough Council was under-borrowed by £1.827m at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2024-25 ADC and WBC - WIP
findings.headline: Adur re-profiled its £43.4m Strategic Property Economic Regeneration Fund out of 2024-25 due to staff resources and extended lead times.
findings.detail: A major regeneration scheme has been delayed. The original capital budget of £86.190m was cut to actual spend of £21.838m, with £43.4m of the Strategic Property Economic Regeneration Fund re-profiled. The council reports that extended lead times and lack of staff resources constrained its ability to deliver projects.
findings.matters: A £43m regeneration scheme at risk of delay raises questions about whether Adur can deliver its economic strategy with current staffing and project management capacity.
findings.figures: £43.4m Strategic Property Economic Regeneration Fund re-profiled; original budget £86.190m, actual spend £21.838m
findings.quote: For Adur, the original budget was revised due to subsequent approvals and re-profiling of budgets, most significantly the reprofiling of the Strategic Property Economic Regeneration Fund (£43.4m) and the impact of extended lead times and staff resources on the ability to deliver some projects.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2024-25 ADC and WBC - WIP
findings.headline: Worthing Borough Council overspent £365.8k on borrowing interest and faces cash shortfall from delayed asset sales.
findings.detail: The council's actual interest costs on borrowing exceeded budget by £365.8k due to sustained elevated interest rates. This was compounded by delays in the disposal of sites from which capital receipts were planned, meaning the council cannot release the cash it expected to reduce borrowing need.
findings.matters: Higher than budgeted interest costs reduce financial headroom. Delays in capital receipts prolong the council's reliance on expensive borrowing and undermine cash planning assumptions.
findings.figures: £365.8k overspend on interest payments; reliance on capital receipts from site disposals that have not materialised
findings.quote: The Council also made an overspend of £365.8k against the budget for interest payments on borrowing, this is in part due to a sustained elevation in interest rates, the pricing of government borrowing within fixed income markets and stubborn inflationary stagnation. This was further compounded by delays in the disposal of sites for which some capital receipts were planned to be received.

news_drafts.headline: Worthing's treasury budget significantly underspent partly because project interest was capitalized to avoid revenue overspend on Integrated Care Centre
news_drafts.lead: Interest capitalization deferred revenue pressure; without it, the council would have faced a £300k overspend on treasury costs, indicating tight affordability margins on this major project

news_drafts.headline: Energy price shock threatens further inflation spike and rate increases: treasury advisors flag risk of CPI breaching 4.5% later in 2026
news_drafts.lead: If energy-driven inflation spike materializes, refinancing costs will be significantly higher than currently budgeted; lenders assess councils' resilience to sustained high rate environment

news_drafts.headline: Interest rate environment sharply reversed from expectation: Bank Rate held at 3.75% and treasury advisors now expect rises to 4-4.25%, not cuts
news_drafts.lead: Refinancing of maturing debt (23-25% of portfolio under 12 months) will occur at materially higher rates than forecast; both councils face higher financing costs and must refinance debt when rates are elevated
